Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-17-energy-dispatch-shortlist.md

# Which batteries belong on the dispatch shortlist?

An energy cooperative needs northern battery sites marked ready with at least 100 kWh available. Six synthetic snapshots include a site exactly at the threshold, one just below it, a southern site, a held site, and an offline site. Operator facets count sites, not stored energy.

Use a fresh `field_note_energy` index on running servers. Curl is the same client for native Elasticsearch, native OpenSearch, and qdrant-es-gateway: change only `ES` to the target endpoint URL.

```sh
ES=http://localhost:19200
curl -fsS -X PUT "$ES/field_note_energy" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"mappings":{"properties":{"site":{"type":"keyword"},"region":{"type":"keyword"},"operator":{"type":"keyword"},"state":{"type":"keyword"},"available_kwh":{"type":"integer"}}}}'
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_energy/_bulk?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-ndjson' --data-binary @- <<'NDJSON'
{"index":{"_id":"battery-101"}}
{"site":"Moor Lane","region":"north","operator":"Aster","state":"ready","available_kwh":120}
{"index":{"_id":"battery-102"}}
{"site":"Quarry Farm","region":"north","operator":"Birch","state":"ready","available_kwh":100}
{"index":{"_id":"battery-103"}}
{"site":"Mill Yard","region":"north","operator":"Aster","state":"ready","available_kwh":99}
{"index":{"_id":"battery-104"}}
{"site":"South Meadow","region":"south","operator":"Birch","state":"ready","available_kwh":180}
{"index":{"_id":"battery-105"}}
{"site":"Hill Barn","region":"north","operator":"Cedar","state":"hold","available_kwh":200}
{"index":{"_id":"battery-106"}}
{"site":"Canal Depot","region":"north","operator":"Cedar","state":"offline","available_kwh":250}
NDJSON
sleep 5
```

Use the same five-second pause after bulk and update on all three servers; this tests settled data, not an immediate refresh guarantee. Find the eligible sites:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_energy/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":10,"query":{"bool":{"filter":[{"term":{"region":"north"}},{"term":{"state":"ready"}},{"range":{"available_kwh":{"gte":100}}}]}}}'
```

Expect `battery-101` and `battery-102`, total `2`, with complete sources; hit order is immaterial. The 100 kWh boundary is inclusive. Count operators over exactly that shortlist:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_energy/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":0,"query":{"bool":{"filter":[{"term":{"region":"north"}},{"term":{"state":"ready"}},{"range":{"available_kwh":{"gte":100}}}]}},"aggs":{"operators":{"terms":{"field":"operator","size":10}}}}'
```

Expect `Aster: 1` and `Birch: 1`, with no hits. Now place Moor Lane on hold without changing its reported capacity:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_energy/_update/battery-101?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"doc":{"state":"hold"}}'
sleep 5
curl -fsS "$ES/field_note_energy/_doc/battery-101"
```

The update returns `updated`; the read shows `state: "hold"` and preserves `site`, `region`, `operator`, and `available_kwh: 120`. Repeat both search requests: only `battery-102` remains, total `1`, with `Birch: 1`. A held site's sufficient energy must not keep it eligible. These snapshots support planning; they do not issue dispatch commands.

Boundary: atomic concurrent energy reservations remain [unsupported](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/compatibility/).

The [fixture](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/fixtures/energy.json) and [replay](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/energy.py) check statuses, bulk IDs/results, every source, exact search IDs/totals, operator counts, and hold exclusion. The [recorded run](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/energy-2026-10-17.json) passed **105/105** checks on Elasticsearch **8.15.0**, OpenSearch **3.9.0**, and gateway **0.2.0** with Qdrant **1.15.5**, using identical requests and embedded sources with synchronous writes. No OpenSearch-specific behavior or difference in these assertions was observed. The [article curl run](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/energy-curl-2026-10-17.json) independently checked all nine responses per engine. No gateway code change or performance claim is involved.

Remove the example index when finished:

```sh
curl -fsS -X DELETE "$ES/field_note_energy"
```


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-17-aws-retail-demo-store-compatibility.md

# AWS Retail Demo Store: compatible search requests, different trade-offs

The [AWS Retail Demo Store](https://github.com/aws-samples/retail-demo-store) is a useful reality check because its search service talks to OpenSearch through the ordinary `opensearch-py` API. Its product search uses `dis_max`, `match_bool_prefix`, category collapse with named `inner_hits`, and `_source: false`. Its similar-products route uses `more_like_this`.

I replayed those request bodies unchanged against native OpenSearch 3.9.0 and this gateway backed by Qdrant 1.19.2. The replay created a settings-only `products` index and wrote individual products, just as the demo's local indexing script does. Both endpoints returned the fields the application consumes, including product IDs, named category hits, and similar-product results that exclude the source product.

## What passed

| Check | OpenSearch | Gateway + Qdrant |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Index, search, and similar-product HTTP contract | Pass | Pass |
| Repeated search p50 at 1K | 5.75 ms | 1.37 ms |
| Repeated search p95 at 1K | 7.10 ms | 2.36 ms |
| Repeated search p50 at 1M | 30.08 ms | 1.63 ms |
| Repeated search p95 at 1M | 33.62 ms | 2.85 ms |
| First similar-product request at 1M | 135.15 ms | 33.04 ms |

The gateway also needed two small compatibility fixes exposed by this replay: settings-only indexes now route dynamically mapped text fields through the catch-all lexical vector, and a missing Qdrant point is treated like a missing Elasticsearch document. The latter matters when `more_like_this` looks up its source document.

## The resource trade-off

These are fresh local Docker volumes, after loading unique generated product names and descriptions and while the indexes were retained. They are footprint snapshots, not a production sizing or cloud-billing benchmark.

| Corpus | Service | CPU snapshot | Memory snapshot | Data volume |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1K | OpenSearch 3.9.0 | 3.83% | 1.090 GiB | 630 KiB |
| 1K | Gateway + Qdrant 1.19.2 | 1.31% combined | 310 MiB combined | 419 MB combined |
| 1M | OpenSearch 3.9.0 | 0.92% | 1.241 GiB | 75.2 MB |
| 1M | Gateway + Qdrant 1.19.2 | 0.08% combined | 581 MiB combined | 876 MB combined |

The negative trade-off is real: Qdrant used more disk. At 1M documents, the gateway-plus-Qdrant volume was about 11.6× the OpenSearch volume. The gateway process itself remained small; Qdrant carries the searchable representation and sparse index. OpenSearch's JVM used more memory in these snapshots, but CPU and memory readings are instantaneous and environment-dependent.

The disk did not grow linearly in this experiment. Moving from 1K to 1M documents increased the OpenSearch volume about 119× and the Qdrant volume about 2.1×. That is evidence of substantial fixed index overhead at the 1K point, not a promise that Qdrant storage is always sublinear. The generator uses five product families with unique names and descriptions; a production catalogue with more varied fields, longer text, replicas, retention, or different sparse-index settings can have a different slope.

I also retried the same 10M-document bulk run after a complete Docker cleanup,
with about 27 GiB free. Qdrant reached roughly 9.57M documents, but the
process was killed for exceeding available memory before the final search could
complete. That is a capacity limit of this test host, not a failed
compatibility assertion, so there is no honest 10M performance number to
publish from this machine. A completed 10M comparison needs more memory.

## What did not become identical

Passing the application contract does not make the two engines rank identically. The native result produced two category groups for the fixture; the gateway produced one bounded candidate group. Scores and similar-product ordering also differ because Qdrant's sparse retrieval is not Lucene/OpenSearch scoring. Refresh timing and the gateway's bounded candidate window remain explicit trade-offs.

So the honest conclusion is narrow: the Retail Demo Store's product-search and similar-product request shapes are a good fit for the gateway, with no application-side URL or response-handling changes in this replay. If exact OpenSearch ranking or category diversity is part of the product contract, validate that separately before migrating.

Reproduce the check with:

```sh
python3 validation/retail_demo.py \
  --native http://localhost:19311 \
  --gateway http://localhost:19313 \
  --docs 1000000 \
  --workers 32 \
  --output validation/evidence/retail-demo-2026-10-17-1m-clean.json
```

The request shapes come from the demo's [search service](https://github.com/aws-samples/retail-demo-store/blob/master/src/search/src/search-service/app.py), and its settings-only indexing flow is shown in [`local_index_products.py`](https://github.com/aws-samples/retail-demo-store/blob/master/src/search/local_index_products.py). The clean 1K and 1M reports are [`retail-demo-2026-10-17-1k-clean.json`](https://dstockton.github.io/validation/evidence/retail-demo-2026-10-17-1k-clean.json) and [`retail-demo-2026-10-17-1m-clean.json`](https://dstockton.github.io/validation/evidence/retail-demo-2026-10-17-1m-clean.json).


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-16-search-controls-cannot-be-decoration.md

# Search controls cannot be decoration

The gateway accepted `min_score`, `terminate_after`, and per-search `timeout` fields but did not apply them. That is more dangerous than a clear unsupported-feature response: a caller could ask to remove low-scoring hits, stop collection early, or return within a deadline and instead receive an ordinary complete page.

Separate ephemeral-container probes exercised Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 with the same one-shard, three-document corpus. `min_score: 2` removed all three `match_all` hits on both engines. `terminate_after: 1` returned one hit with `terminated_early: true` on both, but Elasticsearch reported a total of three while OpenSearch reported one. Both engines accepted `timeout: "1s"`, returned `timed_out: false` for this small request, and rejected the invalid value `"banana"` with HTTP 400. The sanitized [request and response evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/elasticsearch-9.5.5-opensearch-3.9-search-controls-2026-10-16.json) records the versions, images, requests, and observed fields.

The gateway now rejects all three controls before index lookup or Qdrant access. Supporting them requires explicit decisions about score comparability, partial-result behavior, and the Elasticsearch/OpenSearch early-termination total difference; silently choosing one engine's shape would misrepresent the other. The focused regression includes valid-looking values for every field and proves that none reaches the mocked Qdrant endpoint:

```console
cargo test invalid_search_options_fail_before_qdrant_work
```

This is request/response evidence, not a latency benchmark. The one-second timeout did not expire, and the small one-shard corpus does not characterize distributed early termination. Existing searches that omit these fields are unchanged; `_msearch` inherits the same fail-closed validation for each query.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-16-empty-alias-batches-are-not-success.md

# An empty alias batch is not success

The aliases API is an administrative write boundary. The gateway previously treated `{"actions":[]}` as a valid request: it opened and committed an empty catalogue transaction, then returned `{"acknowledged":true}`. A client bug that accidentally dropped every action could therefore look like a completed routing change.

Separate clean-container probes sent the same empty action list and missing action field to Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0. Both engines returned HTTP 400 with `illegal_argument_exception` and the reason `No action specified` for both requests. The sanitized [request and response evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/elasticsearch-9.5.5-opensearch-3.9-empty-alias-actions-2026-10-16.json) records the exact engine versions, images, and observed fields.

The gateway now checks for at least one action before index lookup or the alias handler's catalogue transaction and returns the shared native error shape. In shared-catalog mode, the outer administrative wrapper still loads a snapshot and acquires then releases its claim on this validation error; it does not publish a changed snapshot. A focused regression covers both `{}` and `{"actions":[]}` and proves an existing alias target remains unchanged:

```console
cargo test empty_alias_batches_are_rejected_without_catalogue_changes
```

This is request-level compatibility evidence, not a performance benchmark. It does not claim that every malformed alias body has identical parsing errors: for example, non-array `actions` values continue to use the gateway's structured unsupported-request response. Supported non-empty batches and the documented Elasticsearch/OpenSearch mixed-action response difference are unchanged.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-testing-a-cache-before-building-it.md

# Testing a cache before building it

Would Valkey make this gateway fast enough to beat native search? Before adding
a production cache, we tested a narrower question: **is there enough latency
headroom in an ideal warm hit to justify the work?**

The answer is cautiously useful. A standalone synthetic probe returned aggregation
responses about **7–15% faster** than the faster native engine's median latency
across the corrected measurement rounds. Its aggregation p95 values were also
lower than both native engines in both rounds. This is a reason to investigate,
not a gateway performance win: the production gateway still trailed both native
engines in all ten measured workload/concurrency combinations.

### What the probe actually does

We captured 644 distinct, correctness-checked responses from the real gateway
using the public 10,000-document catalogue. A separate probe validates each
incoming request, hashes its identity and performs one Valkey Lua lookup. The
script checks synthetic control state and returns an already populated response.
The probe parses that response, updates `took` and serializes JSON normally.

Every request is a warm hit. There are no cache misses, changing documents,
invalidation, crash recovery or real writer coordination. Qdrant remains
provisioned but receives no reads on hits. The probe is deliberately named
`cache_probe` in the evidence, rather than “gateway + Qdrant”. It is not a
production feature, and its guard tests do not establish cache consistency.

The combined budget remains two CPUs and 4 GiB: probe 0.5 CPU/512 MiB, Valkey
0.25 CPU/256 MiB, and Qdrant 1.25 CPU/3328 MiB. Each native engine retains two
CPUs and 4 GiB. Normal production rounds instead allocate 0.5 CPU/512 MiB to the
gateway and 1.5 CPUs/3584 MiB to Qdrant. Native caching stays enabled.

### First, fix the measuring instrument

The initial probe run exposed a benchmark problem. For every filter-aggregation
response, the Python verifier recomputed the expected count by walking the entire
corpus. That work sat outside the nominal HTTP timer, but with concurrent clients
it still competed for Python's global interpreter lock and delayed other clients.
Trial throughput also included this verification work.

The corrected harness computes the same expected count once and retains the
strict response assertions. Correctness conclusions did not change. Historical
filter-aggregation timing rows need caution; we retain them with their original
validation profile instead of pooling old and new medians. This identified issue
concerns filter-count validation, not evidence that every historical workload was
invalid.

We then measured two corrected production rounds and two corrected probe rounds,
with native engines interleaved in each. Each profile passed **36,000 measured
response checks**. The earlier 36,000-response probe profile is separately retained.

### The available margin is small

The table gives each corrected probe round separately. Values are median trial
p50 milliseconds, shown as **Elasticsearch / OpenSearch / synthetic probe**.

| Aggregation | Clients | Round 1 | Round 2 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Terms buckets | 1 | 0.360 / 0.347 / 0.307 | 0.362 / 0.354 / 0.315 |
| Two filter counts | 1 | 0.347 / 0.336 / 0.300 | 0.347 / 0.340 / 0.298 |
| Terms buckets | 8 | 0.888 / 0.840 / 0.783 | 0.815 / 0.822 / 0.738 |
| Two filter counts | 8 | 0.795 / 0.811 / 0.673 | 0.780 / 0.786 / 0.700 |

These are optimistic ceilings on potential performance, not a demonstrated
production advantage. Correct write fencing, epoch changes, miss publication and
recovery all have costs. Even a modest extra round trip or a lower hit rate could
erase the observed margin. A broader cache for document reads and sorted pages needs its own correctness
design and production measurements.

The [complete corrected probe summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-cache-ceiling/summary-probe-v2.json)
includes every participant and all five workloads, with p50, p95 and throughput
for both rounds. The [production summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-cache-ceiling/summary-production-v2.json)
shows the actual gateway alongside its own native controls. We have not combined
those separate profiles into an implementation speedup claim.

To reproduce the diagnostic, follow the
[standalone probe instructions](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/benchmark/cache-upper-bound):
capture from the retained production image, build before timing, then measure
with `REQUESTS=200 TRIALS=3 WARMUP=40` and exact totals. Restore the production
image and original Qdrant allocation afterward. The
[evidence manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-cache-ceiling/manifest.json)
records all six raw rounds, separate summaries, image provenance, the fixture
hash and resource budgets.

Valkey now has a measured reason to remain under consideration. The remaining
question is whether a correct cache can preserve enough of this small margin.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-sorted-pages-look-past-first-candidates.md

# Find the next page across the whole catalogue

Sorting the first few candidates is not the same as finding the first few sorted
results. Likewise, asking for a page after price 20 cannot work reliably if the
gateway only fetched records priced below 20.

Filter-only searches with explicit field sorting now inspect every matching
Qdrant scroll page. The gateway keeps the best `from + size` candidates, drops
records before `search_after`, and continues until the scroll ends. Without
collapse, retained hit candidates are bounded by the requested window plus the
current upstream page.

```json
{"size":2,"sort":[{"rank":"asc"}],"search_after":[2]}
```

The six-document [comparison fixture](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/validation/aggregations)
expects records 3 and 4 from that request. It sends the same request to
Elasticsearch and to the gateway. A deterministic regression also puts the
cheapest record on a later page and verifies that it wins the first sorted page.

`post_filter` now scans beyond the initial candidate window too. Matching records
on later pages can fill the requested page, and the hit count covers the complete
post-filtered set. Aggregations continue to see the query before `post_filter`.

Run `cargo test aggregation_scroll_visits_every_page_and_uses_search_projection_values`
to exercise those cases without a running database.

This preserves stateless request handling: no server-side cursor session or Redis
entry is required. The trade-off is scanning matching records for each request.
Use a unique final sort field for predictable cursor boundaries. These changes
apply to filter-only searches; ranked text pagination retains its documented
candidate limits. Collapse still needs retained group members, so its memory cost
is different. Concurrent writes can move records between pages because this is
not a point in time snapshot.

The container replay against Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2 passed all four cases: complete aggregations, post-filtered hits, the first sorted page, and its cursor continuation. The [captured results](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/aggregations/results.json) include actual request timings. They establish correctness for this fixture, not a speed advantage.

A later [three-engine benchmark](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-indexed-query-performance.md)
adds guarded indexed paths for compatible numeric sorting, keyword facets and
simple filter counts. The complete scan described here remains the fallback
when the gateway cannot prove those operations preserve the result.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-sharing-mappings-between-gateway-replicas.md

# Two gateways need one view of their mappings

Adding a second gateway sounds straightforward: start another process and send it traffic. But if each process has its own SQLite file, an alias created through one process is invisible to the other. A restart-safe local database does not automatically become shared metadata.

Qdrant ES Gateway now has an optional Redis/Valkey catalog for that deployment. Mappings, vector names and aliases live in one authoritative store. Each request reads its current committed catalog, so the next request can land on either replica without relying on a local metadata cache. Qdrant continues to store the documents and perform searches.

SQLite remains the default. We have not measured a SQLite bottleneck, and there is no reason to add another service to a single-gateway setup just to replace a small local catalog.

## What changes for an operator

For a new empty deployment, configure `CATALOG_REDIS_URL`, initialize the catalog once with `CATALOG_INITIALIZE=true`, then remove that initialization flag and start the other replicas. Use a persistent, non-evicting Redis/Valkey deployment. Existing SQLite installations need a deliberate migration; simply pointing them at an empty catalog will not discover their mappings.

Administrative changes have one owner at a time. After a successful change, the gateway publishes the metadata and releases ownership atomically within Redis/Valkey. If a gateway crashes while changing a Qdrant collection, it leaves its administrative claim in place. New requests fail closed until an operator reconciles the two stores.

That recovery step is intentional. A lock that expires after thirty seconds does not prove a slow Qdrant request stopped executing. Letting another gateway take over at that point could make the catalog less trustworthy.

## What this does—and what it costs

The shared catalog solves visibility and administrative ownership. It does not turn Qdrant and Redis/Valkey into one transaction, or make concurrent document updates atomic. Nor is this a performance claim: every request fetches a bounded metadata snapshot and builds an ephemeral SQLite view. Large catalogs and high request rates need measurement before adopting this approach.

The real-server test uses two independent clients to verify that metadata becomes visible after commit, concurrent administrators are refused, and a vanished owner does not silently lose its claim. These are correctness checks, not benchmark results.

For configuration, the test command, durability requirements and the recovery procedure, see [the shared catalog guide](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/shared-catalog/). Start with SQLite for one gateway; choose shared metadata when adding replicas creates a real ownership problem.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-shared-cache-warm-search-results.md

# Repeated searches get faster; fresh queries still cost more

The gateway now has a measured advantage for repeated, unchanged searches.
With its optional shared cache enabled, warm search medians were **12–30% lower
than the faster native engine** across our eight search/concurrency comparisons.
Point reads were close to parity, with only a 3–5% combined median advantage.
That advantage was not consistent in every round: in the second enabled round,
single-client point reads were about 2% slower than the faster native engine.

This is the actual gateway, not the earlier synthetic cache probe. It uses Qdrant
for documents and Valkey for shared cache entries, the authoritative catalog and
persistent write coordination. The trade-off is real: fresh queries and
write-followed-by-point-read cycles remained substantially slower than native
Elasticsearch and OpenSearch. This is useful for a read-heavy catalogue with
repeated queries, not a blanket search-engine win.

### Warm searches, same requests

We used Elasticsearch 8.15.0, OpenSearch 3.9.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2 with 10,000
synthetic catalogue documents. Every engine received the same requests and exact
total-hit requirements. Native request caches stayed at their defaults.

The table contains every warm workload. Values are median trial p50 milliseconds,
shown as **one client / eight clients**. All six trial medians from both
cache-enabled rounds contribute; we did not select the fastest trial.

| Operation | Elasticsearch | OpenSearch | Gateway + Qdrant + Valkey |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.350 / 0.707 | 0.345 / 0.661 | 0.333 / 0.630 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.579 / 1.401 | 0.547 / 1.343 | 0.417 / 1.033 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.643 / 1.405 | 0.541 / 1.289 | 0.382 / 1.026 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.460 / 1.081 | 0.453 / 1.136 | 0.360 / 0.951 |
| Two filter counts | 0.416 / 0.981 | 0.409 / 1.057 | 0.339 / 0.800 |

Warm p95 values were also lower than both native engines in these ten cells.
The [complete enabled summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-shared-cache/summary-on.json)
includes p95, throughput and the range of trial medians.

We alternated **serving off, on, on, off**, keeping the same image, data and
resource caps. Write coordination remained enabled in both modes. With serving
off, the gateway's single-client sorted page was 1.362 ms; with serving on it was
0.382 ms. Those off-mode results include the shared-catalog and coordination
architecture, so they do not measure total overhead versus a gateway without
cache infrastructure. The [off-mode summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-shared-cache/summary-off.json)
retains every native control and gateway result too.

### Misses and writes change the answer

We separately tested unused cache keys and real writes. “Cold” here means a new
response-cache key on already loaded data, not cold operating-system caches or
storage. Values below are median trial p50 milliseconds with cache serving on.
Write rows measure the combined write and following read at one client.

| Separate workload | Elasticsearch | OpenSearch | Gateway + Qdrant + Valkey |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| New sorted-filter query, one client | 0.582 | 0.522 | 2.085 |
| New sorted-filter query, eight clients | 1.446 | 1.344 | 5.454 |
| Write then read the document | 1.070 | 1.006 | 2.712 |
| Write then read filter counts | 3.964 | 4.439 | 3.273 |

Misses pay for the Qdrant query and cache publication. The gateway's cold-query
median increased from 1.567 to 2.085 ms at one client when serving was enabled.
At eight clients it increased from 3.993 to 5.454 ms; that enabled run's p95 was
45.499 ms, versus roughly 2.7–2.8 ms for native engines. Tail latency matters as
much as the warm median.

Point-write cycles omit `refresh` for every engine because native GET is
realtime. Filter-count cycles use `refresh=true` everywhere because the next
search requires immediate visibility. The gateway led that latter comparison,
but caching itself did not improve the write cycle: its median rose from
2.942 ms with serving off to 3.273 ms with serving on. Point-write cycles also
rose, from 2.310 to 2.712 ms. These separate off/on profiles were not an ABBA
experiment, so their differences should not be treated as isolated effect sizes.
The [complete mixed-workload summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-shared-cache/summary-mixed.json)
includes all participants, both modes and p95 values.

### The cache has to know when an answer is unsafe

Before a mutation starts, the gateway advances a shared generation and records a
persistent writer token. A cached answer is usable only in the same quiet
generation. A cold read captures that generation before loading metadata; if a
writer intervenes, its result cannot be published into the cache.

The token is released only after backend completion and catalog publication are
known complete. A timeout, cancellation or uncertain operation leaves a fence in
place. That sacrifices cache availability until deliberate recovery instead of
reusing an answer after an unresolved write. Replicas remain stateless, but this
is not a system without state: Valkey's durability and the exclusive writer
contract are essential. Direct Qdrant writes, unfenced gateway replicas and
automatic failover to older coordination state are unsupported.

Every native engine had a two-CPU, 4-GiB cap. The gateway setup shared the same
aggregate budget: gateway 0.5 CPU/512 MiB, Qdrant 1.25 CPUs/3328 MiB, and Valkey
0.25 CPU/256 MiB. Valkey used durable AOF with `appendfsync always` and a 64-MiB
memory limit inside its container. We included its resource and write costs.
An idle post-warm-run memory snapshot totaled approximately 265 MiB for those
three services, versus 984 MiB and 923 MiB for the native engines. These are
single container observations, not peak memory or capacity estimates.

### Reproduce and decide

These results measure revision
[`187944e4cc274a0ae61a6c79de885179319e9d4a`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/187944e4cc274a0ae61a6c79de885179319e9d4a).
Later optimizations require separate measurements; they are not represented by
this baseline. The [harness and full preparation procedure at that revision](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/187944e4cc274a0ae61a6c79de885179319e9d4a/benchmark/shared-cache)
prepare a fresh disposable deployment and reuse the three-engine correctness
checks. Build that revision, run its preparation helper, load the saved deployment
identity into `CACHE_BENCH_DEPLOYMENT`, and select `CACHE_BENCH_SERVE=true` using
the documented Compose command. Once ready, this measures one enabled round:

```sh
ROUND=on-1 REQUESTS=200 TRIALS=3 WARMUP=40 \
  OUTPUT=benchmark/shared-cache/results/on-1.json \
  python3 benchmark/shared-cache/measure.py
# Preserve the other three rounds and run the separate cold/invalidation profiles.
```

Across the retained profiles, **86,400 measured HTTP responses passed correctness
checks**: 72,000 warm reads, 7,200 cold reads and 7,200 responses from 3,600
write/read cycles. Checks cover sources, IDs, ordering, totals, buckets and
changed document contents. The
[evidence manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-shared-cache/manifest.json)
links all eight raw rounds, the exact build, image IDs and resource observations.
These runs use the v3 client-validation profile and are kept separate from older
measurements.

For repeated catalogue searches between writes, the cache offers a demonstrated
latency benefit in this lab profile. For mostly new queries or frequent document
updates, the native engines remain stronger in the measured cases. Start with
your actual reuse and write rate, and follow the
[deployment and recovery requirements](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/shared-read-cache/)
before enabling it.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-rustls-security-fixes-landed.md

# Rustls security fixes landed

The dependency update in [PR #62](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/pull/62) moved Rustls from 0.23.45 to 0.23.46. That patch is now on main. It strengthens the TLS layer used for HTTPS requests and encrypted shared-catalog connections, without changing the gateway's search API.

The [upstream release](https://github.com/rustls/rustls/releases/tag/v/0.23.46) fixes several security issues, including secret data appearing in session debug output and key-exchange hints being saved before a handshake is confirmed. Some other fixes concern optional TLS features; this does not mean every deployment was exposed to every issue.

The merged change passed Rust tests, the dependency audit, Helm checks, and the container build and vulnerability gate. Today's follow-up independently confirmed the locked 0.23.46 version and passed formatting, tests, Clippy, a refreshed dependency audit, and Compose and Helm validation. These checks support the update; they are not a reproduction of each upstream security advisory.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-reusing-catalog-connections.md

# Reusing catalog connections helps misses and writes, with a warm-read warning

The shared catalog was opening a new Valkey connection whenever a request loaded
its metadata snapshot. We changed it to reuse a persistent multiplexed connection.
A failed operation is still returned as a failure: reconnecting later must not
silently replay a write whose outcome is uncertain.

In a new paired experiment, gateway cold-query and write/read medians generally
improved by **12–17%**. The exception was eight-client cold queries with cache
serving off, which improved only 1.4%. Warm performance was mixed, and one
important case regressed. This change reduces connection work; it does not
establish an across-the-board latency improvement.

### Compare within this experiment

We measured the original revision
[`187944e`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/187944e4cc274a0ae61a6c79de885179319e9d4a)
against connection-reuse change
[`49da1cb`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/49da1cb22279d22761e18cb38480c36d0bea943b),
built from validated source
[`c420872`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/c4208725b240289a3c0890e576904b80bdf7a0e7).
Each profile used **old, new, new, old** order, retaining native controls and all
trials. Cache coordination stayed enabled; serving off/on were separate profiles.

Native and old-gateway absolute latency were higher than in the
[earlier shared-cache experiment](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-shared-cache-warm-search-results.md).
We therefore keep these experiments separate. Their differences cannot identify
a cause, and pooling their medians would be misleading.

Values below are gateway median trial p50 milliseconds. Cold means unused
response-cache keys on loaded data. Write rows measure a write and its following
read with one client.

| Workload | Serving off: old → new | Serving on: old → new |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cold sorted filter, one client | 2.590 → 2.159 | 3.155 → 2.788 |
| Cold sorted filter, eight clients | 7.761 → 7.650 | 10.692 → 9.344 |
| Write then point read | 3.524 → 2.914 | 4.008 → 3.392 |
| Write then filter counts | 4.673 → 3.974 | 5.137 → 4.481 |

Median improvements do not describe the whole result. Eight-client cold p95
increased from **64.454 to 71.301 ms** with serving off and **51.765 to 57.449 ms**
with serving on. The new enabled gateway's cold medians remained approximately
4.1 and 4.8 times the faster native engine at one and eight clients. Native
engines also remained faster for write/point-read cycles. The gateway led the
write/filter-count comparison, whose identical `refresh=true` requests require
immediate search visibility; point-write cycles omit refresh on every engine.

### Warm reads were not uniformly preserved

These are the separate cache-enabled warm rounds. Each cell shows **one client /
eight clients**, in milliseconds.

| Gateway operation | Old | New |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.380 / 0.845 | 0.381 / 0.985 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.593 / 1.324 | 0.571 / 1.403 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.603 / 1.344 | 0.462 / 1.411 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.417 / 1.351 | 0.413 / 1.136 |
| Two filter counts | 0.403 / 1.037 | 0.403 / 1.046 |

Eight-client point-read p50 rose **16.5%**, and p95 rose **27.5%**, from 1.242 to
1.583 ms. The native point-read medians also increased roughly 12% between the
corresponding old/new rounds. That drift prevents attributing the gateway change
to connection reuse alone, but it does not make the adverse result disappear.
**Warm-read neutrality remains unproven.**

The [full summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-catalog-transport/summary.json)
includes all native, old-gateway and new-gateway rows, with p95 and throughput.
The new gateway still led the warm search medians in this experiment; native
point reads and the cold/write costs prevent a blanket engine-performance claim.

### Replay the change

The corpus remained 10,000 documents, with identical client requests and v3
correctness assertions. Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 each retained
two CPUs and 4 GiB. Gateway, Qdrant 1.19.2 and durable Valkey shared that same
aggregate budget. No builds ran during timing.

Build both pinned revisions before measuring and prepare the disposable shared
cache deployment using the
[pinned harness instructions](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/c4208725b240289a3c0890e576904b80bdf7a0e7/benchmark/shared-cache).
The retained [round driver](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-catalog-transport/transport_round.py)
and [image override](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-catalog-transport/transport-image.yml)
belong in that harness directory. They replace only the gateway image, wait for
readiness, preserve volumes and refuse to overwrite evidence. Defaults verify the
recorded image IDs before changing the container. For a rebuilt image, pass its
explicit `--old-image-id` or `--new-image-id` and retain the resulting provenance.

Build the old revision as `qdrant-es-gateway:cache-runtime` and the new revision
as `qdrant-es-gateway:catalog-transport`. Fresh local builds generally have different
image IDs from the retained lab images. After verifying their source revisions,
record those local IDs and pass them explicitly:

```sh
old_image_id=$(docker image inspect qdrant-es-gateway:cache-runtime | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]["Id"])')
new_image_id=$(docker image inspect qdrant-es-gateway:catalog-transport | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]["Id"])')
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/transport_round.py off old 1 mixed \
  --old-image-id "$old_image_id" --new-image-id "$new_image_id"
# Keep both ID arguments for each later call.
# Continue off: new 1, new 2, old 2; repeat the four rounds with on.
# Then run on old 1 warm, on new 1 warm, on new 2 warm, on old 2 warm.
```

All **129,600 measured HTTP responses** passed checks across twenty raw rounds.
The [manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-catalog-transport/manifest.json)
records exact image IDs, revisions, every raw file and post-run observations.
Memory snapshots are not peaks, and container-lifetime throttling counters cannot
attribute individual latency changes. Valkey key-access counters are not response-cache
hit rates; the retained observations do not provide a causal diagnosis.
Published raw files add experiment/build labels to prevent accidental pooling;
the manifest preserves their original hashes and identifies that metadata-only
annotation. Connection reuse removes avoidable work
from misses and writes; the warm-read regression and cold tails remain visible
in the evidence.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-request-local-catalog-read-views.md

# Removing request-local SQLite reconstruction: modest gains, one worse tail

The shared-catalog read path used to rebuild an in-memory SQLite database for
every uncached request. Document reads and searches now load the same validated
snapshot into request-local maps. In our paired experiment, cold-query medians
fell **4.5–5.5% with cache serving enabled** and **4.3–7.6% with serving disabled**.
The enabled eight-client p95 worsened **10.5%**. This is a modest reduction in
request overhead, not an across-the-board latency win.

### Change the representation, preserve the boundary

The change applies to exact document GET and index search GET/POST handlers in
shared-catalog mode. It includes requests that bypass the response cache or run
with serving disabled. Each request still obtains a fresh authoritative snapshot,
validates every mapping and vector list, and rejects duplicate records. Concrete
indices retain precedence over single-hop aliases. There is no persistent local
metadata cache or fallback to an old local database.

Metadata and mutation handlers still use SQLite; default local SQLite deployments
are unchanged. Quiet cache misses keep the atomic generation/snapshot operation,
and the original ticket still guards cache publication after an alias or document
change. This remains a full-catalog fetch and validation, bounded at 8 MiB, with
work proportional to catalog size. It does not establish that SQLite generally
limits search performance. The [operational guide](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/shared-catalog/)
describes the scope.

### Cold medians improved, but the enabled tail did not

We compared baseline
[`2deda5e`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/2deda5e43b72de9b2c2ad6f9043df2a01217fd55)
with candidate
[`04b6d7e`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/04b6d7eecce6230634109ec1905509666f00b8bc)
in old, new, new, old order. Serving-enabled and serving-disabled profiles remained
separate; coordination stayed enabled in both. Cold means new response-cache keys
on loaded data. Values below are median trial quantiles in milliseconds.

| Gateway cold sorted filter | p50 old → new | p95 old → new |
|---|---:|---:|
| Serving enabled, one client | 1.911 → 1.826 | 2.374 → 2.201 |
| Serving enabled, eight clients | 4.782 → 4.521 | 55.131 → 60.917 |
| Serving disabled, one client | 1.372 → 1.312 | 1.479 → 1.435 |
| Serving disabled, eight clients | 3.234 → 2.989 | 55.984 → 43.680 |

The enabled eight-client p95 increase repeated in both rounds: baseline round
medians were 55.141/55.121 ms, versus 61.437/60.396 ms for the candidate. The
disabled p95 reduction was less stable: baseline 79.107/25.479 ms versus candidate
32.133/55.227 ms. Cold p50 improvements repeated in both rounds of both modes.
Both native engines remained substantially faster for cold queries. These are
their p50 controls from the same enabled rounds:

| Cold sorted filter | Elasticsearch old → new | OpenSearch old → new |
|---|---:|---:|
| One client | 0.570 → 0.575 | 0.488 → 0.493 |
| Eight clients | 1.255 → 1.251 | 1.169 → 1.265 |

Native movement and the adverse gateway tail rule out a blanket performance claim.
The [complete summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-typed-readview/typed-readview-summary.json)
retains all 42 native and gateway comparisons, including the disabled controls.

### Warm behavior is separate

Warm cache hits do not reconstruct the catalog. Their p50 results were mostly
close, with some reductions and some increases. Cells show one / eight clients.

| Warm gateway operation | Old p50 ms | New p50 ms |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.305 / 0.582 | 0.302 / 0.578 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.386 / 0.954 | 0.388 / 0.900 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.388 / 0.913 | 0.383 / 0.898 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.329 / 0.773 | 0.329 / 0.780 |
| Two filter counts | 0.318 / 0.742 | 0.314 / 0.716 |

Single-client filtered-page p50 rose 0.45%, and eight-client terms p50 rose 0.93%.
Single-client terms p95 rose **4.19%** (0.401 → 0.418 ms); eight-client point p95
rose **1.19%** (0.838 → 0.848 ms). These changes should not be presented as a warm
read improvement caused by removing work from misses.

### Reproduce and inspect

All **93,600 measured responses** passed correctness checks: 72,000 warm,
14,400 enabled cold and 7,200 disabled cold. The corpus contained 10,000 documents,
with unchanged requests, exact totals and validation profile v3. Each profile used
three trials per round, giving six trial quantiles per image for each comparison.
No builds or tests ran during measurement.

Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 each had two CPUs and 4 GiB. Gateway,
Qdrant 1.19.2 and durable Valkey shared that aggregate budget. Qdrant retained its
automatic two/eight search-pool budgets; both profile boundaries reported high-I/O
mode. The driver primes all engines identically before each profile, including
uncached sorted queries, and recreates the gateway consistently between rounds.

Follow the [pinned shared-cache preparation procedure](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/04b6d7eecce6230634109ec1905509666f00b8bc/benchmark/shared-cache).
Build the two revisions as `qdrant-es-gateway:atomic-snapshot` and
`qdrant-es-gateway:typed-readview`. Record their local image IDs; rebuilt images
need not have the historical IDs in the
[manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-typed-readview/manifest.json).
From the repository root after preparation:

```sh
old_id=$(docker image inspect qdrant-es-gateway:atomic-snapshot | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]["Id"])')
new_id=$(docker image inspect qdrant-es-gateway:typed-readview | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]["Id"])')
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/readview_round.py on-main old 1 \
  --old-image-id "$old_id" \
  --new-image qdrant-es-gateway:typed-readview --new-image-id "$new_id" \
  --new-source 04b6d7eecce6230634109ec1905509666f00b8bc
# Repeat on-main new 1, on-main new 2, on-main old 2, keeping all flags.
# Then off-control old 1, new 1, new 2, old 2, keeping all flags.
```

All twelve raw profiles, eight resource records and the exact driver, override
and helpers are retained in the manifest. Only ephemeral container IDs were
removed; original and published hashes are recorded. Resource intervals cover
profile setup and native-engine phases as well as gateway work. Qdrant was
throttled in roughly 15.8–20.6% of its cold-profile scheduling periods and none
of the warm-profile periods. These counters do not explain individual requests.
No AOF rewrite increments or delayed fsync were recorded within sampled profile
intervals. A rewrite completed between the final baseline cold and warm snapshots
(the cumulative count rose from two to three). The second enabled candidate cold
profile recorded 43.949 ms of Valkey throttling. These observations remain in the
evidence rather than being excluded from the comparison.

These measurements are separate from earlier experiments. The read view removes
avoidable reconstruction while keeping complete validation and request-local
metadata. The modest median gains, worse enabled tail and native cold-query
advantage all remain part of the result.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-qdrant-search-thread-tradeoff.md

# One Qdrant search thread improves tails, but hurts typical cold queries

Limiting Qdrant search pools to one thread produced a clear trade-off in our small
CPU-budget experiment. With eight clients, gateway cold-query p95 fell from
**45.610 to 11.088 ms**, while p50 rose from **4.805 to 7.568 ms**. That is a
75.7% reduction in the tail measurement and a 57.5% increase in typical latency.
Throughput rose 20.1%. It is not an overall latency win or a reason to change
the default everywhere.

### Why test one thread?

Qdrant had a 1.25-CPU quota in our two-CPU gateway deployment. Its telemetry
reported two high-CPU search threads and eight high-I/O search threads, with
high-I/O mode selected. In Qdrant 1.19.2, the automatic budgets are the detected
CPU count and four times that count. An explicit `max_search_threads` sets each
pool's budget instead; it does not cap every thread in the process.
See the versioned [runtime implementation](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/blob/v1.19.2/lib/storage/src/content_manager/toc/runtimes.rs#L34-L115)
and [default calculation](https://github.com/qdrant/qdrant/blob/v1.19.2/lib/common/common/src/defaults.rs#L87-L103).

The pinned CPU-detection library rounds fractional cgroup quotas upward, subject
to available CPUs: 1.25 becomes two here. That explains the reported two/eight
budgets. A CPU quota limits scheduled CPU time, not worker count; extra workers
can be useful while waiting for I/O. These facts motivated a measurement, not an
assumption that fewer workers must be faster.
[CPU detection source](https://github.com/seanmonstar/num_cpus/blob/v1.17.0/src/linux.rs#L201-L215).

### Cold queries: better tails, worse medians

We ran automatic, one, one, automatic order, retaining native controls and all
trials. Only Qdrant's search-thread setting changed. Each value below is the
median of six trial quantiles, in milliseconds. Cold means unused response-cache
keys on loaded data, not cold OS caches or storage.

| Cold sorted filter | Automatic p50 → one | Automatic p95 → one |
|---|---:|---:|
| Gateway, one client | 1.970 → 2.172 | 2.314 → 2.452 |
| Gateway, eight clients | 4.805 → 7.568 | 45.610 → 11.088 |
| Elasticsearch, one client | 0.578 → 0.610 | 0.658 → 0.702 |
| Elasticsearch, eight clients | 1.264 → 1.334 | 2.323 → 2.835 |
| OpenSearch, one client | 0.481 → 0.491 | 0.595 → 0.571 |
| OpenSearch, eight clients | 1.162 → 1.169 | 2.305 → 2.169 |

Both native engines remained faster for these cold queries. Single-client gateway
p50 also worsened, by 10.3%. The eight-client tail improvement does not erase those
costs. Eight-client cold throughput increased from **849.210 to 1,019.941 requests
per second**, using the same median-of-trials calculation. Valkey completed an AOF rewrite during the second one-thread cold profile;
we retain that possible confounder rather than attributing every change to threads.

### Warm reads stayed mixed

The gateway image and enabled response cache were unchanged. These rows show
p50 for one client / eight clients, in milliseconds.

| Warm gateway operation | Automatic | One |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.301 / 0.580 | 0.300 / 0.573 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.371 / 0.916 | 0.391 / 0.940 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.389 / 0.908 | 0.388 / 0.910 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.326 / 0.788 | 0.326 / 0.772 |
| Two filter counts | 0.311 / 0.733 | 0.315 / 0.722 |

Most movements were small. Filtered-page p50 rose 5.3% with one client and 2.7%
with eight; single-client p95 rose 13.6%. Two-filter single-client p95 rose 9.1%.
The [full summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-qdrant-search-threads/summary.json)
includes all 36 native and gateway comparisons and their tails. These warm
observations do not establish a benefit from a setting that acts on backend work.

### Reproduce the comparison

All **86,400 measured responses** passed correctness checks: 14,400 cold and
72,000 warm. The corpus had 10,000 documents. Requests, exact totals, validation
profile v3 and native cache settings stayed the same. Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and
OpenSearch 3.9.0 each had two CPUs and 4 GiB. Gateway, Qdrant 1.19.2 and durable
Valkey shared that aggregate budget: 0.5, 1.25 and 0.25 CPUs respectively.

Use the [shared-cache preparation procedure](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/2deda5e43b72de9b2c2ad6f9043df2a01217fd55/benchmark/shared-cache)
and the gateway source at that revision. Copy the retained
[round driver](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-qdrant-search-threads/thread_round.py),
[image override](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-qdrant-search-threads/thread-image.yml)
and [snapshot helper](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-qdrant-search-threads/snapshot_round.py)
into `benchmark/shared-cache/`. The driver pins the historical
`qdrant-es-gateway:atomic-snapshot` image. A fresh build may have a different ID:
verify its source, explicitly update the driver's `DIGEST` to that local image ID,
and ensure `SOURCE` records the revision actually built. Retain any driver changes
with your results. Do not bypass image verification.

From the repository root, after preparation:

```sh
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/thread_round.py auto 1
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/thread_round.py one 1
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/thread_round.py one 2
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/thread_round.py auto 2
```

The driver restarts Qdrant and the gateway in the same sequence each round,
retains volumes, checks readiness and verifies effective pool budgets. Before each
profile it primes all three engines with identical workloads and additional
uncached sorted queries, outside timing. Collections had 10,000 points and two
segments after each restart. Pool telemetry remained high-I/O at the sampled
boundaries, with budgets two/eight or one/one as intended. Boundary samples do
not prove that no transitions occurred between them.

The [manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-qdrant-search-threads/manifest.json)
links all eight raw profiles, four resource records, image provenance and hashes.
Resource intervals include priming and native-engine phases; throttling counters
cannot assign a cause to individual latency changes. Qdrant cold-profile throttled
time fell from 1.054/0.912 seconds in the automatic rounds to 8.407/3.609
milliseconds in the one-thread rounds. The second one-thread cold profile also
recorded 262.916 ms of Valkey throttling and the AOF rewrite. Those observations
provide context, not a per-request diagnosis. Delayed-fsync counts remained
zero. Only ephemeral container IDs were removed from public evidence.

This experiment stays separate from earlier gateway code comparisons. One search
thread is a possible tail-latency trade-off for this workload and quota, with a
substantial median cost. It is not a generally faster configuration.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-missing-alias-removals-are-not-success.md

# Missing alias removals are not success

The gateway used to acknowledge every syntactically valid alias removal, even when the alias did not exist or belonged to another index. That made a stale deployment or rollover request look successful while leaving the catalogue unchanged. The risk is operational rather than cosmetic: a caller can continue believing that an old read or write route was detached.

Separate clean-container probes exercised Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 with the same requests. Both returned HTTP 404 with `aliases_not_found_exception` for a single missing alias and for an alias attached to a different index. Both also applied the successful add in a mixed missing-remove plus add batch and returned HTTP 200. Their response bodies diverged: Elasticsearch reported `errors: true` and one result per action, while OpenSearch returned only `{"acknowledged":true}`. The sanitized [request and response evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/elasticsearch-9.5.5-opensearch-3.9-alias-remove-2026-10-15.json) records the versions and observed shapes.

The gateway now tracks whether any action in its supported single-target subset can succeed before opening the SQLite transaction. When every removal misses, it returns the shared native 404 shape and leaves the catalogue unchanged. A mixed batch still commits its successful action and returns 200. Exact idempotent adds count as successful, matching native behavior.

```console
cargo test alias_removal_reports_when_no_action_can_succeed
```

This is deliberately not a claim of identical partial-failure responses. The gateway retains the simpler OpenSearch-shaped success body for mixed batches and does not yet emit Elasticsearch per-action alias results. It also continues to reject `must_exist`, alias arrays and patterns, filters, routing, write-index flags, and multi-index final states rather than approximating them. The probe measures request semantics only; it is not a latency or resource benchmark.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-measuring-the-gateway-request-timeline.md

# Measure the request timeline before rewriting JSON handling

The gateway's own diagnostic traces show that backend waiting occupies most of
the measured cold-search dispatch interval. The median **per-request** fraction
spent in the backend join was **79.4% with one client and 73.6% with eight**.
Cache-envelope JSON parsing took a single-client median of **0.017 ms**, compared
with **1.162 ms** for the whole dispatch interval. These traces do not justify a
JSON-handling rewrite as the next optimization.

This is an instrumented diagnostic, not a production performance benchmark or a
native-engine comparison. The `diagnostic-timing` compile-time feature is off by
default. Its timers, trace storage and response header add overhead.

### Follow the actual request

We captured 600 correct sorted-filter responses: 100 cold, 100 warm and 100
explicitly bypassed requests at each of one and eight clients. Each request keeps
exact totals and returns 20 full-source documents in rank order. The corpus has
10,000 documents. Cold bounds were ranks 1–100 with one client and 301–400 with
eight, so the exact counts include most of the corpus. Warm profiles repeat bounds
101 and 401; bypass profiles use bounds 201–300 and 501–600. These selectivities
matter when comparing this diagnostic with another workload.

The following values are per-phase p50 milliseconds for cold requests:

| Interval | One client | Eight clients |
|---|---:|---:|
| Complete dispatch scope | 1.162 | 2.513 |
| Cache lookup | 0.059 | 0.223 |
| Catalog read-view parsing | 0.002 | 0.001 |
| Backend join | 0.916 | 1.708 |
| Work after the join | 0.044 | 0.040 |
| Response JSON encoding | 0.013 | 0.011 |
| Cache-envelope parsing | 0.017 | 0.015 |
| Cache-envelope encoding | 0.006 | 0.005 |
| Cache publication | 0.088 | 0.277 |

**These rows overlap and must not be added.** Response encoding sits inside the
work after the join; the join includes concurrent count, coverage and ordered-page
RPCs plus their local response handling. The fractions above were calculated for
each individual request before taking the median, not by dividing table medians.

The count RPC finished last among those three operations in **100 of 100**
single-client cold requests and **86 of 100** eight-client cold requests. Ordered
response parsing had medians of **0.015 / 0.016 ms**. That makes backend work a
better-supported investigation target than JSON parsing for this workload. It
does not prove the count endpoint is the only cost or that dropping exact totals
would preserve the same request contract.

Warm dispatch medians were 0.092 / 0.228 ms; bypass medians were 1.018 / 2.080 ms.
The [full phase summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-gateway-phases/gateway-phases-summary.json)
and [per-request relationships](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-gateway-phases/gateway-phases-relationships.json)
retain every profile, including tails. Profiles ran in a fixed order and are not
paired speed comparisons.

### What the clocks include

Dispatch timing excludes HTTP request-body ingress, final diagnostic-header
serialization and network delivery. Client-observed cold p50 was 1.500 / 3.442 ms;
subtracting those independent medians would not measure a specific overhead.
The RPC send-to-headers interval includes connection-pool waits, socket work,
backend execution and scheduling. Body receipt and parsing have separate nested
intervals. Wall intervals are not CPU measurements.

Resource snapshots include untimed worker connection primers. A zero rounded
microsecond interval does not mean work is free. The trace records no request
bodies, credentials or backend URLs. Production builds omit the timing header.

### Reproduce the diagnostic, then restore production

The diagnostic image was built from
[`68add4d`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/68add4dc8aecd8b01ad501ee30ab4d94518f03b6)
with `diagnostic-timing` enabled. The runner is pinned separately in the
[manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-gateway-phases/manifest.json),
which also contains both image identities and the restoration record.
Use the prepared shared-cache corpus and resource settings from that revision:
gateway 0.5 CPU/512 MiB, Qdrant 1.25 CPUs/3,328 MiB and Valkey 0.25 CPU/256 MiB.
Qdrant keeps its automatic two/eight pool budgets and cache serving is enabled.

In an isolated checkout of the diagnostic source, build its dedicated image:

```sh
docker build -f benchmark/shared-cache/diagnostic.Dockerfile \
  -t qdrant-es-gateway:phase-diagnostic .
```

Copy the retained [runner](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-gateway-phases/gateway_phases.py)
and [Compose override](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-gateway-phases/phase-image.yml)
into `benchmark/shared-cache/`. Load `CACHE_BENCH_DEPLOYMENT` from the preparation
file, set `CACHE_BENCH_SERVE=true`, and use `PHASE_GATEWAY_IMAGE` with the existing
three-engine/shared-cache Compose files plus the override to recreate only the
gateway. Wait for readiness before capture. Record the locally built image ID:

```sh
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/gateway_phases.py \
  --image-id '<full locally verified diagnostic image ID>' \
  --source 68add4dc8aecd8b01ad501ee30ab4d94518f03b6
```

The runner requires fresh cold keys and refuses to overwrite evidence. For another
capture, use a new prefix and an unused `--start` range; retain that changed
selectivity. It does not deploy or restore images. After capture, recreate the
gateway with the retained production image and verify readiness and the absence
of diagnostic headers. Our [restoration record](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-gateway-phases/gateway-phases-restoration.json)
confirms production was restored with cache serving enabled.

All raw traces, resource observations, runner copies and hashes are retained;
public records remove only ephemeral container IDs. No additional performance
claim follows from instrumenting the path. The useful result is a better basis
for choosing the next correctness-preserving experiment.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-measuring-small-read-path-changes.md

# Fewer requests did not make this query faster

> Measurement note: these historical filter-aggregation trials recomputed the expected count in each client worker. The calculation was outside that request's timer, but affected throughput and could delay concurrent requests. Later trials tagged `precomputed-filter-count-v2` compute it once before timing. The figures here are preserved without adjustment; do not combine them with the corrected trials.

We tried to speed up gateway aggregations by combining their safety checks.
Two filter counts would need four Qdrant calls instead of five, including the
exact total. That sounded promising. After measuring the final implementation,
we removed it: fewer calls did not produce a reliable latency improvement, and
filter counts were slightly slower.

This followed our [indexed-query optimization](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-indexed-query-performance.md).
The large win there came from avoiding a complete document scan. The next round
was about much smaller costs: database query preparation, duplicated payloads,
and coordination between independent reads.

### Compare the code, not the warmup

Fresh runs changed the ranking even when the gateway binary stayed identical.
We therefore kept the same 10,000 documents and alternated the old and new
images in **old, new, new, old** order. Each round shuffled Elasticsearch,
OpenSearch and gateway + Qdrant trials, used persistent connections, and warmed
each workload before measuring it. No image builds ran during these trials.

The retained read-path change passed **72,000 measured response checks** across
four rounds. That includes full sources, IDs, ordering, exact totals and buckets.
Each variant contributes six trial medians to each table cell; values are
**one client / eight clients**, in milliseconds.

| Gateway operation | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.380 / 0.781 | 0.370 / 0.783 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.702 / 2.055 | 0.688 / 2.037 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 1.022 / 2.613 | 1.009 / 2.521 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.892 / 3.382 | 0.896 / 3.159 |
| Two filter counts | 1.109 / 3.332 | 1.129 / 3.283 |

These small, mixed differences do not establish a broad speedup. Native engines
remained faster in all ten workload/concurrency combinations in this warmed
comparison. The [complete summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-read-path/summary.json)
includes their results, p95 latency, throughput and trial ranges.

### What we kept

Document reads now ask Qdrant only for the payload fields they consume. For one
representative benchmark document, the internal payload shrank from **684 to
274 bytes**, while the returned source stayed identical. Bulk existence checks
request only document IDs. GET and HEAD no longer parse unused mapping metadata;
SQLite reuses prepared statements, and parsing happens outside the catalog lock.
The final search page also takes ownership of its hits instead of copying them.

These remove specific work without a result cache or another service. Alias
changes still take effect immediately: prepared statements cache query plans,
not catalog answers. The evidence supports reduced data movement; it does not
support a promised percentage improvement in application latency.

### What we rejected

The combined aggregation check required a more complicated backend predicate.
Review also caught an intermediate-memory problem with launching every facet at
once. We bounded concurrency and reduced responses immediately, then reran the
comparison. The final result still did not justify the extra complexity, so the
original aggregation path remains. CPU redistribution, one runtime worker and
an exploratory in-memory payload configuration also failed to establish a
consistent benefit; their defaults remain unchanged.

Native caching matters, but it is not the whole explanation. Both native engines
recorded roughly 18,000 request-cache hits and three misses. [Elasticsearch](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/shard-request-cache.html)
and [OpenSearch](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/search-plugins/caching/request-cache/)
cache eligible aggregation requests by default.
A separate `request_cache=false` diagnostic left those counters unchanged, yet
native engines remained faster. Adding Redis without locating the remaining
cost would not by itself solve that difference.

### Reproduce the read comparison

Build both gateway revisions before timing, load the shared corpus using the
[three-engine runner](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/benchmark/three-engine),
and replace only the gateway image between rounds. Retain the data volumes and
wait for readiness after each replacement.

```sh
ROUND=baseline-a REQUESTS=200 TRIALS=3 WARMUP=40 \
  OUTPUT=results/baseline-a.json python3 compare_reads.py
# Repeat with candidate-b, candidate-c and baseline-d.
python3 summarize_reads.py results/baseline-a.json results/baseline-d.json
python3 summarize_reads.py results/candidate-b.json results/candidate-c.json
```

Every engine receives the same requests; the original aggregate two-CPU, 4-GiB
limits remain. The [evidence manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-read-path/manifest.json)
identifies revisions, raw round files, image IDs and the rejected experiment.
This remains an investigation, not a claim that the gateway has overtaken the
native engines.

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-library-large-print-availability.md

# Can I borrow the large-print edition today?

A public-library reader wants a large-print book available at York today. A standard edition of the same title, an ebook, a copy at Leeds, and a fully borrowed title should stay out. These six synthetic holdings represent one title/format/branch combination per document; no borrower data is needed.

Use running Elasticsearch-compatible servers and a fresh `field_note_library` index. Curl is the client: run these same commands against each server, changing only `ES` to the gateway URL (for example, `http://localhost:9200`).

```sh
ES=http://localhost:19200
curl -fsS -X PUT "$ES/field_note_library" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"mappings":{"properties":{"title":{"type":"text"},"branch":{"type":"keyword"},"format":{"type":"keyword"},"genre":{"type":"keyword"},"available_copies":{"type":"integer"}}}}'
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_library/_bulk?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-ndjson' --data-binary @- <<'NDJSON'
{"index":{"_id":"book-101"}}
{"title":"The Harbour Mystery","branch":"York","format":"large-print","genre":"crime","available_copies":1}
{"index":{"_id":"book-102"}}
{"title":"A Garden in Winter","branch":"York","format":"large-print","genre":"fiction","available_copies":2}
{"index":{"_id":"book-103"}}
{"title":"The Harbour Mystery","branch":"York","format":"standard","genre":"crime","available_copies":3}
{"index":{"_id":"book-104"}}
{"title":"Mountain Letters","branch":"York","format":"large-print","genre":"biography","available_copies":0}
{"index":{"_id":"book-105"}}
{"title":"River Detectives","branch":"Leeds","format":"large-print","genre":"crime","available_copies":2}
{"index":{"_id":"book-106"}}
{"title":"Summer on the Moors","branch":"York","format":"ebook","genre":"fiction","available_copies":4}
NDJSON
sleep 5
```

The same five-second settling pause is used on both endpoints; it does not establish immediate gateway refresh visibility.

Find the available large-print holdings at York:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_library/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":10,"query":{"bool":{"filter":[{"term":{"branch":"York"}},{"term":{"format":"large-print"}},{"range":{"available_copies":{"gte":1}}}]}}}'
```

Expect exactly `book-101` (The Harbour Mystery) and `book-102` (A Garden in Winter), total `2`, with their complete sources; hit order is immaterial. Count titles by genre over that same filtered selection:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_library/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":0,"query":{"bool":{"filter":[{"term":{"branch":"York"}},{"term":{"format":"large-print"}},{"range":{"available_copies":{"gte":1}}}]}},"aggs":{"genres":{"terms":{"field":"genre","size":10}}}}'
```

Expect `crime: 1` and `fiction: 1`, with no hits. These buckets count holdings records, not copies: the two available copies of A Garden in Winter contribute one fiction record.

The lending system now reports that the final large-print copy of The Harbour Mystery has been borrowed. Publish its new availability and read the record back:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_library/_update/book-101?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"doc":{"available_copies":0}}'
sleep 5
curl -fsS "$ES/field_note_library/_doc/book-101"
```

The update returns `updated`; the read retains the title, branch, format and genre, with `available_copies: 0`. Repeat both searches above: only `book-102` remains, total `1`, and the sole genre bucket is `fiction: 1`. The standard edition of The Harbour Mystery must not substitute for the borrowed large-print edition.

The [fixture](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/fixtures/library.json) and [replay](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/library.py) verify HTTP statuses, bulk IDs/results, every stored source, exact search totals, genre counts and last-copy exclusion. The [recorded run](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/library-2026-10-15.json) passed 70/70 checks on Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and gateway 0.2.0 with Qdrant 1.15.5, using identical requests, embedded sources and synchronous writes. The article's curl requests were also executed on both endpoints. No gateway code change or performance claim is involved.

Boundary: updates are not [atomic concurrent reservations](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/compatibility/); the lending system remains authoritative for loans.

Remove the example index when finished:

```sh
curl -fsS -X DELETE "$ES/field_note_library"
```
