Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-inside-a-cold-search-backend-diagnostic.md

# Inside a cold search: a backend diagnostic, not another engine benchmark

After reducing cache-fill overhead, we inspected three Qdrant operations used by
a filtered, sorted search: exact counting, checking indexed-field coverage, and
retrieving an ordered page. The diagnostic found that exact counting had the
largest single-client server-reported time of those operations. It also showed a
large gap between server-reported timings and parallel client wall time under
concurrency. Neither observation identifies the entire gateway bottleneck.

**This is not an Elasticsearch-compatible or native-engine comparison.** The
runner sends Qdrant RPCs directly inside the container network. It bypasses the
gateway, catalog, response cache and public client path. Its Python client is
not the gateway's Rust client.

### Three pieces of work

The requests use a range filter over the retained 10,000-document corpus. The
count is exact. The coverage probe asks whether any matching document lacks the
expected indexed-field marker. The ordered request retrieves 21 full-source documents with their document IDs
in ascending rank order. All results are checked, including counts, ordering,
document IDs and full sources.

A separate [payload-schema snapshot](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-backend-diagnostic/backend-payload-schema.json)
captured **after the diagnostic** found an integer index on `rank` and a keyword
index on the coverage marker, each covering all 10,000 points. It does not support
a missing-rank-index explanation for the observed count cost, but it is not
contemporaneous proof of the index state during timing.

These are pooled p50 **Qdrant response `time` fields**, in milliseconds, from
400 measured calls per configuration:

| RPC | Run alone, one / eight clients | Run in parallel, one / eight clients |
|---|---:|---:|
| Exact count | 0.698 / 0.892 | 0.734 / 0.873 |
| Coverage probe | 0.163 / 0.298 | 0.180 / 0.320 |
| Ordered page | 0.136 / 0.190 | 0.170 / 0.263 |

The parallel group waits for all three operations and includes Python dispatch,
JSON parsing and correctness validation. Its median trial p50/p95 was
**1.023 / 1.161 ms with one client** and **4.426 / 41.780 ms with eight clients**.
Per-RPC client wall time ends when the response body is received; it has a different
boundary from both group time and the server's reported field.

Do not add parallel quantiles or subtract these independently aggregated timings
to estimate gateway overhead. Network transit, client scheduling, executor work,
validation and server queueing can contribute at different boundaries. This
experiment does not isolate their individual costs or prove count is the sole
bottleneck. The [full summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-backend-diagnostic/backend-decomposition-summary.json)
retains standalone and parallel group quantiles plus each RPC's client and
server-reported quantiles.

### Resource context and reproducibility

All **4,800 measured RPC responses across 3,200 groups** passed checks. Four trials
rotate the operation order at each concurrency level. Connections are persistent
per worker and RPC. The isolated Python generator has two CPUs and 256 MiB,
outside the server budget; its execution model can influence group wall time.

Qdrant 1.19.2 retained 1.25 CPUs and 3,328 MiB. The collection was green at both sampled boundaries, with
10,000 points and two segments. Search-pool telemetry reported high-I/O mode and
two/eight pool budgets at both boundaries. Across the whole capture, Qdrant was
throttled in **13 of 32 scheduling periods (40.6%)**, with **1.107 seconds** of
reported throttled time. Other recorded services had no throttled periods.
These whole-run counters do not assign the long parallel tail to a particular
request or exclude client effects.

Use the [prepared harness at revision 47113fc](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/47113fc5a0bc1f3ab4aad6728a480626c7aa006f/benchmark/shared-cache)
with its retained corpus and resource settings. Copy the
[launcher](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-backend-diagnostic/backend_diagnostic.py)
and [RPC runner](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-backend-diagnostic/backend_decomposition.py)
into `benchmark/shared-cache/`, then run from the repository root:

```sh
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/backend_diagnostic.py --prefix backend-decomposition
```

The launcher requires the recorded Python image digest to be available, checks
the prepared corpus and resource limits, and refuses to overwrite evidence.
It creates a restricted temporary runner without changing the engines. The
[manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-backend-diagnostic/manifest.json)
records the image provenance, exact runner hashes, raw samples and resource
snapshots. The two diagnostic scripts were uncommitted at execution; their exact
copies are retained. The gateway image was built from `47113fc`, but the gateway
was not in this measured request path. Only ephemeral container IDs were removed
from public records.

The next useful question is which changes reduce complete request latency while
preserving exact counts and result correctness. These measurements help choose
experiments; they are not evidence of a new production speedup.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-indexed-query-performance.md

# Sorting twenty records should not fetch ten thousand

> Measurement note: these historical filter-aggregation trials recomputed the expected count in each client worker. The calculation was outside that request's timer, but affected throughput and could delay concurrent requests. Later trials tagged `precomputed-filter-count-v2` compute it once before timing. The figures here are preserved without adjustment; do not combine them with the corrected trials.

Our first three-engine benchmark exposed a straightforward problem. To return
20 sorted products, the gateway fetched all 10,000 matching documents from
Qdrant. It also fetched those documents to count a handful of categories.
The answers were correct, but moving and reducing all that data was expensive:
median sorted-page latency was 55.6 ms, and terms aggregation took 39.1 ms.
Elasticsearch and OpenSearch completed those operations in roughly 1–2 ms.

We changed where the work happens. For compatible numeric fields, Qdrant now
orders the records and returns the requested page. Keyword buckets use exact
Qdrant facets; simple filter counts use its count API. Independent reads run
concurrently, and a count-only request does not fetch an unused document.
No client request changes, result cache, or Redis/Valkey service were needed.

Each cell shows **one client / eight clients**, in milliseconds.

| Operation | Elasticsearch | OpenSearch | Gateway + Qdrant |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.466 / 1.194 | 0.428 / 1.047 | 0.502 / 1.298 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 1.023 / 2.960 | 0.939 / 3.251 | 0.917 / 3.190 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.948 / 2.263 | 0.733 / 2.602 | 1.228 / 3.565 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.586 / 1.996 | 0.605 / 1.791 | 1.068 / 4.302 |
| Two filter counts | 0.714 / 2.928 | 0.718 / 2.854 | 1.135 / 4.167 |

These are median trial p50 latencies in milliseconds, measured with one and
eight concurrent clients. Every measured response passed correctness checks:
IDs, full sources, sort values, exact totals, bucket order and counts. We kept
all trials, including slower ones. The [full summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15/summary.json)
contains p95 latency, throughput and the range of trial medians.

The optimized gateway reduced observed sorted-page latency to 1.228 ms,
about 45 times lower than the first run. Native engines also became faster
across runs, so that ratio is an observed before/after result, not an isolated
production speedup guarantee. The gateway narrowly led filtered search at one
client; that small margin is not a broad performance win. In this measured run, native engines had lower median latency in nine of the ten
workload/concurrency combinations. They also led searchable ingest throughput: roughly
31,900 documents/s for Elasticsearch, 41,600 for OpenSearch and 22,600 for the
gateway.

The clearer advantage was the observed memory footprint. During separate
five-second, eight-client filter-count probes, gateway + Qdrant used about
327 MiB, versus 973 MiB for Elasticsearch and 912 MiB for OpenSearch. Those are
single Docker memory observations, not peaks or production sizing estimates.
For a compact catalogue service already using Qdrant, this is a useful trade:
near-millisecond scalar queries with a smaller observed footprint. For the
lowest latency or fastest ingest in this profile, the native engines remain
stronger choices.

There is a correctness condition behind the speedup. New writes record which
fields have values the indexed operation can handle exactly. Queries check that
coverage before using the fast result. Old documents, mixed types, missing
numeric values, multiple sort fields and page-boundary ties use the complete
scan. Existing documents gain eligibility when rewritten; deploying the new
binary alone does not accelerate every old index. Existing indexes that already
own the new internal field retain their
original data and behavior. This remains stateless request processing; it does
not turn pagination into a snapshot during concurrent writes.

### Reproduce the comparison

The [container profile and runner](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/benchmark/three-engine)
use Elasticsearch 8.15.0, OpenSearch 3.9.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2. Each native engine
has a two-CPU, 4-GiB cap; Qdrant and the gateway share the same total cap. Both
JVM heaps are 512 MiB. The dataset has 10,000 deterministic documents with
integer rank/price fields, 20 keyword categories and a description. All engines
receive the same mapping, documents and requests; only the endpoint changes.
This tests scalar catalogue operations, not text relevance or vector search.

```sh
cd benchmark/three-engine
docker compose -p qeg-balanced -f compose.yml up -d --build
# Once all three endpoints respond:
DOCS=10000 TRIALS=3 REQUESTS=40 CONCURRENCY=1,8 python3 run.py
python3 summarize.py results/three-engine.json
```

The runner uses persistent HTTP connections, warms each workload, shuffles engine
order with a fixed seed, and measures three trials of 40 requests. Bulk timings
include waiting until all documents are searchable. It deletes only its named
benchmark index, so use the disposable containers. All services share one Docker
VM; this is a small reproducible lab profile, not a production capacity estimate.

Download the [baseline trials](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15/baseline.json),
[optimized trials](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15/optimized.json) and
[build/resource provenance](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15/provenance.json).
The practical improvement is that compatible catalogue queries move a page or
counts across the network instead of the entire matching catalogue. SQLite was
not the measured bottleneck, so replacing its small metadata catalog would not
have addressed the expensive work this benchmark revealed.

A [later paired comparison](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-measuring-small-read-path-changes.md)
examines warmup, native caches and smaller read-path changes.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-explicit-sparse-vectors-without-token-folding.md

# Keep your sparse token IDs intact

A sparse embedding is a small dictionary: token IDs paired with weights. If the
same token changes identity between indexing and searching, a successful HTTP
response can hide the wrong answer.

An [OpenSearch report](https://github.com/opensearch-project/neural-search/issues/2048)
describes exactly that problem in the SEISMIC approximate path of OpenSearch
3.9.0: “the query token is folded, the document tokens are not.” The report also
says the Lucene exact path returns the correct results.

The gateway now accepts explicit sparse embeddings and passes their numeric IDs
to Qdrant unchanged. IDs such as `32768`, `65535` and `65536` stay distinct.
Documents and queries share the same validation: canonical decimal IDs in the
unsigned 32-bit range and positive, finite float32 weights. Invalid vectors fail
before document writes. You supply embeddings; the gateway does not run a model.

Create a field with the common OpenSearch mapping shape:

```json
{"settings":{"index.sparse":true},"mappings":{"properties":{"v":{"type":"sparse_vector","method":{"name":"seismic","engine":"lucene"}}}}}
```

Index a document containing `{"v":{"65536":1.0}}`, then search:

```json
{"size":10,"query":{"neural_sparse":{"v":{"query_tokens":{"65536":1.0}}}}}
```

Qdrant executes an exact sparse dot product. The method labels in the mapping
are accepted compatibility syntax, not a request to run Lucene inside Qdrant.
Engine-specific tuning and model inference are rejected with a 400 response.

We checked the common request shape against real OpenSearch 3.9.0 and Qdrant
1.19.2. Eight documents used tokens `0`, `1`, `32767`, `32768`, `40342`, `65535`,
`65536` and `105878`. Every query returned exactly its own document on both
endpoints. This is a correctness check, **not a reproduction of the reported
approximate-path bug** or a speed comparison.

To repeat it from the repository checkout:

```sh
docker compose -f examples/explicit-sparse/compose.yml up -d --build
# Wait for both endpoints to answer GET /.
python3 examples/explicit-sparse/compare.py
docker compose -f examples/explicit-sparse/compose.yml down -v
```

The [demo and captured results](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/examples/explicit-sparse)
include the complete fixture and individual timings. The script sends identical
requests to both endpoints, changing only the endpoint address. It replaces its
own demo index, so run it against disposable instances.

For an application already using Qdrant, this adds an OpenSearch-shaped way to
search precomputed embeddings without another inference service or gateway
session store. It does not establish that migrating from OpenSearch is better:
the tested native exact path is correct too. Sparse queries currently support a
single top-level field and bounded `from`/`size`; total hits are a lower bound.
They reject aggregations, sorting, collapse, post-filtering, `min_score` and
`search_after`. Scalar filters on the sparse field also fail explicitly.
Use a new index when adding sparse fields to an existing mapping.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-disposable-cache-fills-durable-coordination.md

# Keep coordination durable, let response-cache fills be disposable

A response cache should be cheap to refill. Our cache entries shared Valkey's
append-only log with catalog metadata and writer coordination, so filling a cold
response also added durable log traffic. We changed only response publication to
skip incremental AOF propagation. Catalog updates, generations and writer tokens
retain their required durability.

In a paired experiment, enabled cold-query p50 improved about **21%** at both
one and eight clients. Eight-client p95 fell **67.8%**, from **43.949 to 14.169 ms**.
Native engines still handled these cold queries faster, and warm results included
regressions. The improvement is specific to this cache-fill workload.

### Disposable entries, durable authority

The publication script validates the deployment, generation and quiet writer state
before storing a bounded response with an expiry. It disables propagation only
around that response write, then restores normal propagation. Administrative
claims, catalog publication and writer admission/release keep the existing
`appendfsync always` requirements.

This does not mean response entries can never survive a restart. An AOF rewrite
or snapshot can capture entries already in memory. A restored entry must still
pass identity, build/configuration, generation, expiry and writer-state checks.
An old response cannot become current merely because a rewrite saved it.
The [deployment guide](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/shared-read-cache/) explains these
boundaries. This is not a guarantee that every fill avoids all fsync activity.

### Cold-query results and log growth

We compared baseline
[`04b6d7e`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/04b6d7eecce6230634109ec1905509666f00b8bc)
with measured candidate
[`a778a35`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/a778a357f677345939e61b559bf6beac234624d7),
using old, new, new, old order in separate serving-enabled and serving-disabled
profiles. These measurements describe those builds, not a later merge.
Values are median trial quantiles in milliseconds.

| Gateway cold sorted filter | p50 old → new | p95 old → new |
|---|---:|---:|
| Serving enabled, one client | 1.943 → 1.537 | 2.277 → 1.715 |
| Serving enabled, eight clients | 4.578 → 3.614 | 43.949 → 14.169 |
| Serving disabled, one client | 1.353 → 1.359 | 1.515 → 1.562 |
| Serving disabled, eight clients | 3.336 → 3.150 | 44.380 → 50.073 |

The enabled cold profiles added **9,103,721 and 9,103,723 bytes** to the baseline
AOF, compared with **2,016 bytes in each candidate round**. Disabled cold profiles
also added 2,016 bytes; warm profiles added none. No rewrite occurred within these
sampled intervals, so log compaction does not account for that difference.
The observations support reduced incremental log work, not a count of individual
fsync calls or proof that all latency variation has one cause.

Native cold p50 controls from the enabled rounds remained lower:

| Cold sorted filter | Elasticsearch old → new | OpenSearch old → new |
|---|---:|---:|
| One client | 0.579 → 0.581 | 0.487 → 0.498 |
| Eight clients | 1.201 → 1.295 | 1.247 → 1.182 |

The disabled eight-client p95 worsened **12.8%**, even though response fills were
bypassed. Native controls also moved. Those results remain in the
[complete 42-row summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-ephemeral-publish/ephemeral-publish-summary.json).

### Warm results were mixed

Warm hits do not publish another response. Cells show one / eight clients, in
p50 milliseconds.

| Warm gateway operation | Old | New |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.302 / 0.585 | 0.305 / 0.567 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.396 / 0.911 | 0.387 / 0.914 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.374 / 0.923 | 0.395 / 0.905 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.328 / 0.776 | 0.331 / 0.778 |
| Two filter counts | 0.321 / 0.768 | 0.322 / 0.709 |

Single-client sorted pagination worsened **5.8% at p50 and 21.7% at p95**
(0.439 → 0.535 ms). Eight-client terms p95 rose **5.15%** (1.210 → 1.272 ms).
We do not claim a general warm-read improvement from this change.

### Check crashes as well as speed

An isolated Valkey 8.1.10 proof exercised the production Lua scripts. Publishing
a response produced a hit while AOF size stayed **257 → 257 bytes**. The final
six-check run also verified persistent unresolved claims and writers, durable
catalog commit and releases, rewrite-restored entries with their original expiry,
rejection after a durable generation change, and writer durability after a
publication error.

The [final proof](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-ephemeral-publish/aof-proof-3.json)
and [proof script](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-ephemeral-publish/cache_ephemeral_aof.py)
are retained. So are both earlier attempts: the first failed before checks because
the harness mishandled INFO JSON readiness parsing; the second passed an earlier
five-check suite. They are not silently discarded or presented as equivalent to
the final proof.

### Replay the comparison

All **93,600 measured HTTP responses** passed correctness checks: 72,000 warm,
14,400 enabled cold and 7,200 disabled cold. Each comparison uses six trial
quantiles per image. The 10,000-document corpus, requests, exact totals and
validation profile v3 stayed fixed. Cold means new cache keys on loaded data.

Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 each had two CPUs and 4 GiB. Gateway,
Qdrant 1.19.2 and durable Valkey shared the same aggregate budget. Qdrant retained
automatic search pools. The driver consistently recreates the gateway and primes
all engines outside timing. No builds or tests ran during measurement.

Follow the [pinned preparation instructions](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/a778a357f677345939e61b559bf6beac234624d7/benchmark/shared-cache).
Build the baseline as `qdrant-es-gateway:typed-readview` and candidate as
`qdrant-es-gateway:ephemeral-publish`, using the revisions above. Record local
image IDs; rebuilt images may differ from the historical manifest. After preparation:

```sh
old_id=$(docker image inspect qdrant-es-gateway:typed-readview | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]["Id"])')
new_id=$(docker image inspect qdrant-es-gateway:ephemeral-publish | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]["Id"])')
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/ephemeral_round.py on-main old 1 \
  --old-image-id "$old_id" \
  --new-image qdrant-es-gateway:ephemeral-publish --new-image-id "$new_id" \
  --new-source a778a357f677345939e61b559bf6beac234624d7
# Repeat on-main new 1, new 2, old 2, retaining all flags.
# Then off-control old 1, new 1, new 2, old 2, retaining all flags.
python3 tests/cache_ephemeral_aof.py --output /tmp/cache-aof-proof.json
```

The [manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-ephemeral-publish/manifest.json)
retains twelve raw profiles, eight resource records, all proof attempts, exact
scripts and hashes. Public records omit only ephemeral container identifiers and
failed-proof resource names. Resource counters span setup and native phases as
well as gateway requests; they cannot attribute individual latencies. No delayed
fsync increments were recorded in sampled profiles. Earlier experiments are kept
separate.

For a workload that repeatedly fills the cache, disposable publication removes
unnecessary durable response storage while preserving durable coordination.
That benefit coexists with the native engines’ cold-query advantage and the adverse
warm results above.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-disabling-totals-should-not-slow-sorting.md

# Asking for less should not make sorting slower

> Measurement note: these historical filter-aggregation trials recomputed the expected count in each client worker. The calculation was outside that request's timer, but affected throughput and could delay concurrent requests. Later trials tagged `precomputed-filter-count-v2` compute it once before timing. The figures here are preserved without adjustment; do not combine them with the corrected trials.

A client that only needs the next page can set `track_total_hits: false` and
avoid asking for the total number of matching documents. In the gateway, that
apparently cheaper request had an expensive surprise: it disabled indexed
sorting and fetched every matching document from Qdrant instead.

On our 10,000-product catalogue, a single-client sorted page took **45.340 ms**.
After separating the sorting decision from the total-count decision, the same
request took **0.689 ms**. Both requests return the same twenty products, source
fields and sort values, with no `hits.total` field.

### Keep the page, skip the count

The gateway now uses its guarded indexed sorting path whether or not totals are
requested. When totals are disabled, it skips the exact count. A zero-size
aggregation response also skips the otherwise unused hit lookup. These are
request-local changes: no result cache, new database or Redis service is needed.

The existing safety checks still apply. Eligible scalar numeric fields can use
Qdrant's indexed ordering; unsupported values, old documents without eligibility
metadata and ambiguous page-boundary ties keep the complete-scan fallback.
Disabling totals does not relax sorting correctness or provide snapshot isolation
while documents change.

We measured **old, new, new, old** images against the same retained corpus. Each
image contributes six trial medians per table cell. Values below are median
trial p50 milliseconds, shown as **one client / eight clients**.

| Gateway operation, totals disabled | Before | After |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.384 / 0.842 | 0.374 / 0.769 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 2.888 / 10.093 | 0.691 / 1.797 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 45.340 / 305.877 | 0.689 / 1.833 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.870 / 2.470 | 0.675 / 1.970 |
| Two filter counts | 1.102 / 3.305 | 0.858 / 2.954 |

The point-read request is unaffected by the totals option; its smaller movement
helps show ordinary measurement variation. The large sorting improvement removes
an identified full scan. It does **not** establish that the gateway is faster
than the native engines.

### Native engines still lead

All three engines received identical requests within this disabled-total profile;
only the endpoint changed. Here are the final candidate-round results, including
every workload rather than selecting the gateway's strongest result.

| Operation | Elasticsearch | OpenSearch | Gateway + Qdrant |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.307 / 0.599 | 0.289 / 0.579 | 0.374 / 0.769 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.487 / 1.082 | 0.468 / 1.020 | 0.691 / 1.797 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.554 / 1.185 | 0.442 / 1.028 | 0.689 / 1.833 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.355 / 0.863 | 0.354 / 0.856 | 0.675 / 1.970 |
| Two filter counts | 0.446 / 2.745 | 0.494 / 2.745 | 0.858 / 2.954 |

Both native engines remain faster in all ten workload/concurrency combinations.
For applications already using Qdrant, this fix makes requesting only a page
substantially more practical. It is not a reason to promise lower latency than
Elasticsearch or OpenSearch.

We separately repeated the four-round comparison with exact totals enabled.
That profile passed another 72,000 response checks, with no material measured
regression: single-client filtered search changed from 0.699 to 0.701 ms and
sorted pagination from 1.010 to 1.011 ms. Exact totals and disabled totals are
separate profiles; we did not give the gateway a cheaper request than its peers.
Across both profiles, **144,000 measured responses passed** checks for IDs, full
sources, ordering, bucket counts, and either exact totals or their absence.

### Reproduce it

Use the [three-engine harness](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/benchmark/three-engine)
with Elasticsearch 8.15.0, OpenSearch 3.9.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2. Build both gateway
images before timing and populate the disposable 10,000-document corpus once.
Each native engine has a two-CPU, 4-GiB cap; Qdrant and the gateway share the same
total cap. Native cache settings remain at their defaults.

```sh
# From benchmark/three-engine, after loading data and waiting for readiness:
TRACK_TOTAL_HITS=false ROUND=old-1 REQUESTS=200 TRIALS=3 WARMUP=40 \
  OUTPUT=results/old-1.json python3 compare_reads.py
# Replace only the gateway image, preserving volumes, and wait for readiness.
# Repeat as new-1, new-2, then old-2.
python3 summarize_reads.py results/old-1.json results/old-2.json
python3 summarize_reads.py results/new-1.json results/new-2.json
# Repeat all four rounds with TRACK_TOTAL_HITS=true into separate output files.
```

Each round interleaves all engines, uses persistent connections and warms every
trial. No builds or ingestion run during timing. The shared Docker host and small
scalar catalogue limit what these measurements establish; this is not a text,
vector, durability or production-capacity benchmark.

The [evidence manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-disabled-totals/manifest.json)
links all eight raw rounds, revisions and image provenance. Separate summaries
retain [disabled-total results](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-disabled-totals/disabled-summary.json)
and [exact-total results](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-disabled-totals/exact-summary.json),
including p95 latency, throughput and trial ranges. The improvement is concrete:
a client asking for less work no longer accidentally triggers a full scan.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-changing-transport-was-not-enough.md

# Changing transport was not enough

> Measurement note: these historical filter-aggregation trials recomputed the expected count in each client worker. The calculation was outside that request's timer, but affected throughput and could delay concurrent requests. Later trials tagged `precomputed-filter-count-v2` compute it once before timing. The figures here are preserved without adjustment; do not combine them with the corrected trials.

After removing unnecessary scans, we tested another plausible optimization:
send gateway reads to Qdrant over gRPC instead of REST. The smaller typed
messages and shared connection might reduce overhead. The results were mixed,
so we removed the prototypes and kept REST in production.

### Compare one change at a time

We built each prototype once, then ran the same image with gRPC disabled and
enabled. The client-facing requests, retained 10,000-document corpus and resource
caps stayed identical. Four rounds ran in **REST, candidate, candidate, REST**
order, with Elasticsearch and OpenSearch interleaved throughout. No builds or
ingestion ran during timing.

The first prototype moved supported document reads, scrolling, facets and counts
to gRPC. It improved nine of ten median-latency combinations by roughly 1–11%,
but single-client filter aggregation became **15.4% slower: 1.085 → 1.251 ms**.
Those extra costs mattered more than an attractive count of winning cells.

We then tried a hybrid: keep counts on REST and use gRPC for the other supported
reads. The table shows all gateway results for that second experiment. Each cell
is median trial p50 milliseconds, **one client / eight clients**, using all six
trial medians per variant.

| Operation | REST | Hybrid |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.377 / 0.784 | 0.371 / 0.703 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.703 / 2.017 | 0.706 / 1.851 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 1.015 / 2.519 | 0.990 / 2.531 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.901 / 3.080 | 0.928 / 2.744 |
| Two filter counts | 1.117 / 3.211 | 1.145 / 3.273 |

Five combinations improved and five regressed. Keeping counts on REST reduced
the earlier single-client regression, but did not produce a consistent win.
These are observations from separate paired experiments, not proof that one
transport operation alone caused every difference.

Both native engines remained faster in all ten candidate workload/concurrency
combinations in each experiment. We did not change their requests or disable
their default caching to make the gateway look better.

### Keep the evidence, not the extra machinery

Across the two paired experiments, **144,000 measured responses passed strict
checks** for full sources, IDs, sort values, exact totals and aggregation results.
Correctness was necessary, but it did not justify the additional adapter,
conversion rules and dependencies for these mixed latency results. The gateway
continues to use REST; no new transport setting is required.

This does not establish that gRPC is generally slower, or that it cannot help a
different workload. It shows that changing transport was insufficient to close
this gateway's measured latency gap on a small scalar catalogue. The larger
[disabled-total sorting improvement](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-disabling-totals-should-not-slow-sorting.md)
came from eliminating work rather than changing its encoding.

The [evidence manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-transport/manifest.json)
retains all eight rounds, exact image IDs, resource limits and replayable prototype
patches. Complete summaries include native results, p95 latency, throughput and
trial ranges for the [full gRPC experiment](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-transport/full-summary.json)
and [hybrid experiment](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-transport/hybrid-summary.json).
A separate REST-only disabled-total diagnostic is retained but excluded from the
paired results.

To replay, apply one archived patch and its companion module to the manifest's
base revision, build the image, and use the three-engine read-only runner with
`REQUESTS=200 TRIALS=3 WARMUP=40 TRACK_TOTAL_HITS=true`. Alternate only the backend
transport between rounds, preserving data and waiting for readiness. The native
versions remain Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and OpenSearch 3.9.0, with Qdrant 1.19.2;
each engine receives the same aggregate two-CPU, 4-GiB limit. This is a reproducible
lab experiment, not a production-capacity or general engine ranking.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-calendar-days-follow-local-time.md

# A reporting day is not always 24 hours

A sales report grouped by London day should move its boundaries when the clocks
change. Adding 86,400 seconds to yesterday's boundary gets that wrong twice a year.

The gateway now supports a small, explicit `date_histogram` subset: calendar days,
Monday-starting weeks, months, and years in an IANA time zone. It converts each
timestamp into local calendar time and converts that calendar boundary back to UTC.

```json
{"size":0,"aggs":{"sales_days":{"date_histogram":{"field":"date","calendar_interval":"day","time_zone":"Europe/London","min_doc_count":1}}}}
```

The deterministic test measures 23 hours between the March 29 and March 30, 2026
London boundaries and 25 hours between October 25 and October 26. Documents with
multiple timestamps count once per bucket. Run:

```sh
cargo test calendar_days_follow_dst_and_weeks_start_monday
```

The [comparison fixture](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/validation/aggregations)
contains dates on both sides of those transitions and sends identical requests to
Elasticsearch and the gateway. This is compatibility work for teams already using
Qdrant; there is no claimed speed advantage over a native calendar histogram.

Only nonempty buckets are supported, so `min_doc_count:1` is required. Custom
formats, fixed intervals, offsets, bounds, subaggregations, and nonexistent local
midnight boundaries fail explicitly. Input dates accept epoch milliseconds,
RFC3339 timestamps, and `YYYY-MM-DD` dates. Date-only input denotes midnight UTC.

Time-zone rules come from the compiled `chrono-tz` dependency. Keeping that data
current still matters: implementing a calendar reducer does not repair stale rules.
This does **not** claim to resolve the
[Graylog OpenSearch tzdata report](https://github.com/Graylog2/graylog2-server/issues/27755),
which describes "events near midnight land on the wrong day" under outdated rules.
That reported deployment needs separate reproduction with its exact engine and
updated zone data. The London checks exercise established DST rules, not those
reported Canadian and Moroccan rule changes.

The container replay against Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2 passed all four cases: complete aggregations, post-filtered hits, the first sorted page, and its cursor continuation. The [captured results](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/aggregations/results.json) include actual request timings. They establish correctness for this fixture, not a speed advantage.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-atomic-cache-miss-snapshots.md

# One fewer catalog request, without a proven latency win

A quiet cache miss now gets its generation ticket and catalog snapshot in one
Valkey operation. This removes a second metadata request before querying Qdrant.
In our paired test, cold-query medians fell **3.0% with one client and 7.9% with
eight clients**. Native controls moved too, and warm reads were mixed. These
measurements do **not** isolate a performance win from the change.

### Keep the ticket and snapshot together

The catalog maps index and alias names to collections. The cache ticket identifies
the generation under which a response may be stored. If an alias changes between
independent reads, pairing an older catalog with a newer ticket could allow an
outdated response into the cache.
The previous two-call path already enforced safe ordering by obtaining the ticket
before the catalog. This change preserves that guarantee with one call; it does
not fix a stale-cache bug in the previous path.

The new script checks that no writers are active, captures the generation and
reads the catalog atomically. It bounds the catalog size before fetching its
contents. The gateway loads those bytes through its existing validated SQLite
catalog loader; malformed or duplicate records fail before reaching Qdrant.

A writer starting afterward changes the generation, preventing the earlier
response from filling the cache. That request may still return its response.
This protects cache publication; it does not create a transaction spanning
Valkey and Qdrant or provide backend snapshot isolation. Warm hits retain their
existing path. Busy or failed lookups, and corrupt cached responses, use the
ordinary catalog path.

### What changed in the measurements

We compared the retained connection-reuse image with
[`2deda5e`](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/commit/2deda5e43b72de9b2c2ad6f9043df2a01217fd55),
using old, new, new, old order. Cache-enabled rounds measured cold then warm
queries. A separate serving-off control measured cold queries only; coordination
remained enabled. Cold means unused response-cache keys on loaded data, not cold
OS caches or storage. There were no timed write/read cycles in this experiment.

Each value is the median of six trial p50 measurements, in milliseconds. Native
columns are controls from the same enabled rounds; only the gateway image changes.

| Cold sorted filter | Gateway old → new | Elasticsearch old → new | OpenSearch old → new |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| One client | 4.268 → 4.139 | 1.375 → 1.516 | 1.202 → 1.117 |
| Eight clients | 16.067 → 14.800 | 3.343 → 3.087 | 3.324 → 2.946 |

At eight clients, Elasticsearch improved 7.7% and OpenSearch 11.4%, despite neither
engine changing. Gateway p95 barely moved: **5.099 → 5.122 ms** with one client
and **70.192 → 68.663 ms** with eight. Both native engines remained substantially
faster for these cold queries. Serving-off gateway p50 moved **2.677 → 2.707 ms**
and **10.851 → 10.581 ms**, providing another indication of variation.

Warm results also varied. Cells below show one client / eight clients.

| Warm gateway operation | Old p50 ms | New p50 ms |
|---|---:|---:|
| Read one document | 0.519 / 1.392 | 0.569 / 1.230 |
| Filtered, sorted page | 0.759 / 2.426 | 0.643 / 2.251 |
| Page after a sort cursor | 0.700 / 2.649 | 0.694 / 2.165 |
| Keyword terms buckets | 0.536 / 1.799 | 0.546 / 1.736 |
| Two filter counts | 0.527 / 1.725 | 0.506 / 1.664 |

Single-client point reads worsened **9.6% at p50 and 39.7% at p95**
(0.730 → 1.020 ms). Terms p95 also worsened at both concurrency levels, by 10.7%
and 7.4%. The first baseline warm profile included an AOF rewrite; later profiles
did not. Native controls drifted too. We retain that confounder and every adverse
result rather than attributing warm changes to an optimization that targets misses.
The [complete summary](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-atomic-snapshot/atomic-snapshot-summary.json)
contains all 42 native and gateway comparisons, including p95.

### Replay this experiment

All **93,600 measured HTTP responses** passed the existing correctness checks:
72,000 warm, 14,400 enabled cold and 7,200 serving-off cold. Fifteen smoke-test
operations are recorded separately. The corpus was 10,000 documents with identical
client requests, exact totals and validation profile v3. Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and
OpenSearch 3.9.0 each had two CPUs and 4 GiB. Gateway, Qdrant 1.19.2 and durable
Valkey shared the same aggregate budget. No builds ran during timing.

Use the [pinned preparation procedure](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/2deda5e43b72de9b2c2ad6f9043df2a01217fd55/benchmark/shared-cache)
to create the disposable deployment and its preparation file. Build the baseline
from source `c4208725b240289a3c0890e576904b80bdf7a0e7` as
`qdrant-es-gateway:catalog-transport` and the candidate from `2deda5e` as
`qdrant-es-gateway:atomic-snapshot`. Record each locally built image ID; fresh
builds need not match the historical IDs in the
[manifest](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/assets/benchmarks/2026-10-15-atomic-snapshot/manifest.json).
Then, from the repository root:

```sh
old_id=$(docker image inspect qdrant-es-gateway:catalog-transport | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]["Id"])')
new_id=$(docker image inspect qdrant-es-gateway:atomic-snapshot | python3 -c 'import json,sys; print(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]["Id"])')
python3 benchmark/shared-cache/snapshot_round.py on-main old 1 \
  --old-image-id "$old_id" \
  --new-image qdrant-es-gateway:atomic-snapshot --new-image-id "$new_id" \
  --new-source 2deda5e43b72de9b2c2ad6f9043df2a01217fd55
# Repeat with on-main new 1, on-main new 2, on-main old 2.
# Then off-control old 1, new 1, new 2, old 2, keeping all flags.
```

The manifest links all twelve raw measurement files, eight resource records,
smoke checks, summaries and the retained driver/override. Resource counters span
setup, priming and native-engine phases; they cannot attribute individual request
latency. AOF rewrites advanced from zero to one during the first baseline warm
profile, while delayed-fsync counts remained zero. Ephemeral container IDs were
removed from public records; original hashes and unchanged timing data are retained.

These results remain separate from earlier experiments. Tests demonstrate that
a quiet miss avoids the second catalog fetch without weakening generation checks.
The latency evidence supports a smaller request path, not a broad performance claim.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-aggregations-beyond-the-first-page.md

# The cheapest item may be on the next page

A price filter should describe the matching catalogue, even when the shopper only
asks for one product. The gateway previously calculated `min`, `max`, and filter
counts from the hit candidates it had fetched. A small `size` could therefore
produce a plausible but incomplete answer.

The fix separates those two jobs. Qdrant scrolls through every matching page;
the gateway retains the current extrema and bucket counters, then discards each
page. The hit limit no longer sets the scope of an aggregation. `post_filter`,
collapse, and `search_after` still affect hits, not aggregation membership.

For example:

```json
{"size":0,"aggs":{"lowest_price":{"min":{"field":"price"}},"brands":{"terms":{"field":"brand","size":2}}}}
```

Our regression puts prices 50 and 2 on separate pages. The result is 2, including
when the search returns no hits. Terms now count the complete matching set too,
deduplicate repeated values within one document, and report the actual count
outside the returned top buckets.

Run `cargo test aggregation_scroll_visits_every_page_and_uses_search_projection_values`
for the deterministic two-page check. The repository's
[`validation/aggregations` comparison](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/tree/main/validation/aggregations)
also sends the same six-document fixture and requests to Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and
the gateway with Qdrant. It prints the observed results and individual timings.

This improves correctness within the gateway's supported subset; it is not a
claim that scanning is faster than Elasticsearch's native aggregations. A full
scan costs work proportional to the matching data. Metrics use constant state;
buckets have an explicit 10,000-distinct-value limit per aggregation and fail
rather than return truncated totals. There are at most 100 aggregations per request.

Ranked text and pattern queries are rejected when combined with aggregations,
because their candidate membership cannot currently be reduced exactly this way.
Concurrent writes can change a scroll while it runs. With document projection,
reductions use mapped non-text values in the search projection, keeping membership
and values together instead of fetching a newer source document.

The container replay against Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and Qdrant 1.19.2 passed all four cases: complete aggregations, post-filtered hits, the first sorted page, and its cursor continuation. The [captured results](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/aggregations/results.json) include actual request timings. They establish correctness for this fixture, not a speed advantage.

A later [three-engine benchmark](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-indexed-query-performance.md)
adds guarded indexed paths for compatible numeric sorting, keyword facets and
simple filter counts. The complete scan described here remains the fallback
when the gateway cannot prove those operations preserve the result.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-15-a-shared-catalog-is-not-a-snapshot.md

# A shared catalog is not a snapshot

Moving metadata out of a gateway process makes replicas easier to run. It does not make every Elasticsearch consistency promise available.

A `search_after` cursor describes where the next page should start. If documents change between pages, the next request sees those changes. A point-in-time search needs a retained view of the data, or retained results with clearly defined creation semantics. Saving a cursor in Valkey does not create that view.

The same distinction matters for writes. An `if_seq_no` and `if_primary_term` pair asks the engine to reject a write if the document changed. Checking a value in Redis and then writing to Qdrant is two operations across two systems. A failure or competing writer between them can break the promise. A fast key-value store cannot make them one transaction.

The gateway now rejects point-in-time search bodies and consistency-sensitive URL parameters before executing a request. For example, `PUT /products/_doc/1?if_seq_no=0&if_primary_term=1` returns a structured `400` instead of silently performing an unconditional write. Explicit routing, external versions, scroll contexts, and conflict retries are also rejected when supplied as URL parameters. The focused tests check encoded parameter names as well as ordinary requests.

This keeps the boundary visible while shared metadata and stateless query translation improve. Atomic concurrent document updates still need an authoritative conditional-write mechanism and recovery design. Full Lucene phrase semantics need positional indexing. Neither is supplied by adding a metadata cache.

For applications that use only the supported subset, Qdrant can remain the document and retrieval engine while gateway replicas keep no durable local catalog. Applications requiring snapshot pagination or concurrent compare-and-set writes should retain their native engine for those operations until the gateway can demonstrate the same guarantee.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-14-index-names-are-a-client-contract.md

# Index names are a client contract

An invalid index name used to make it through the gateway's metadata catalogue and into a normalized Qdrant collection name. That was more than cosmetic. An application could successfully provision state that the same Elasticsearch or OpenSearch client would expect a native cluster to reject, and distinct punctuation could then collide in Qdrant's namespace.

Elasticsearch and OpenSearch implement their validators independently, so this change checked both rather than assuming the fork still behaved like its ancestor. [Elasticsearch 9.5.5's validator](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v9.5.5/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/metadata/MetadataCreateIndexService.java#L342-L365) and [OpenSearch 3.9's validator](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/blob/3.9/server/src/main/java/org/opensearch/cluster/metadata/MetadataCreateIndexService.java#L313-L342) agree on the static boundary:

- a name must be non-empty and lowercase;
- filesystem-reserved punctuation, `#`, and `:` are forbidden;
- `_`, `-`, and `+` cannot be the first character;
- the UTF-8 encoding cannot exceed 255 bytes; and
- `.` and `..` are invalid.

The byte boundary matters for non-ASCII names: 127 copies of `é` occupy 254 UTF-8 bytes and pass, while 128 copies occupy 256 bytes and fail. The source implementations permit `+` away from the first character, despite the current OpenSearch prose documentation listing `+` among generally forbidden characters. The gateway follows the versioned 3.9 implementation for that edge rather than broadening the rejection.

Invalid create requests now return HTTP 400 with the client-recognizable `invalid_index_name_exception`, root cause, index name, and `_na_` index UUID. Validation runs under the existing index-administration lock but before SQLite reads and Qdrant requests. Focused regressions cover the UTF-8 byte limit, punctuation, prefixes, lowercase requirement, response shape, and a zero-request mock upstream counter:

```console
cargo test index_name_validation_matches_shared_native_rules
cargo test invalid_index_creation_fails_before_qdrant_work
```

This run is source- and request-level validation, not a live-engine benchmark. The local Docker service did not answer its availability check, so no native containers were claimed. Dot-prefixed names other than the exact `.` and `..` remain accepted by both versioned static validators; their separate hidden/system-index checks and deprecation behavior are not emulated by the gateway.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-14-alias-options-must-not-disappear.md

# Alias options must not disappear

The gateway deliberately implements unfiltered, unrouted aliases with one concrete target. Its alias action parser previously read only `index` and `alias`, but silently ignored every other metadata field. A request for a tenant filter, custom routing, or a write index could therefore return `{"acknowledged":true}` while the stored alias exposed all documents and routed every operation normally. That is more dangerous than an unsupported-feature error because the response tells the caller that a data-access or write-routing boundary exists when it does not.

Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 expose the same relevant action fields, but they were checked independently. The versioned [Elasticsearch request parser](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v9.5.5/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/action/admin/indices/alias/IndicesAliasesRequest.java#L98-L108) accepts `filter`, `routing`, `index_routing`, `search_routing`, `is_write_index`, and `is_hidden` for add actions, plus `must_exist` for removals. The versioned [OpenSearch request parser](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/blob/3.9.0/server/src/main/java/org/opensearch/action/admin/indices/alias/IndicesAliasesRequest.java#L106-L116) declares the corresponding fields, and the separate [OpenSearch alias documentation](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/api-reference/alias/aliases-api/) describes their effects. This is source-level evidence for the two engines, not an assumption that verification against one applies to the other.

The gateway now rejects every action metadata field outside its supported `index` and `alias` subset. Known native options and unknown fields receive a structured HTTP 400 naming the exact path, such as `_aliases.add.filter` or `_aliases.remove.must_exist`. Validation happens before index lookup and before the SQLite transaction, so a rejected request cannot create, remove, or modify an alias and never contacts Qdrant.

```console
cargo test alias_actions_reject_options_the_gateway_cannot_apply
```

The regression covers filters, all three routing forms, write-index and hidden flags, removal `must_exist`, and an unknown option. It also asserts that the catalogue still contains only its original alias after all failures. Docker was not responsive during this run, so no live Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Qdrant endpoint result is claimed. This change does not add filtered, routed, hidden, or multi-index aliases; it makes the existing compatibility boundary honest and fail closed.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-13-support-first-reply-queue.md

# Who is still waiting for a first reply?

A support lead needs open billing tickets with no replies and no assigned agent. Seven synthetic tickets include assigned, answered, closed, and technical cases that must stay out of the queue. Missing and null assignees qualify; an empty string counts as present, so producers should normalize blank assignments to null.

Use running Elasticsearch-compatible servers and a fresh `field_note_support` index. Curl is the client: run these commands on each server, changing only `ES` to the gateway URL (for example, `http://localhost:9200`).

```sh
ES=http://localhost:19200
curl -fsS -X PUT "$ES/field_note_support" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"mappings":{"properties":{"subject":{"type":"text"},"team":{"type":"keyword"},"status":{"type":"keyword"},"channel":{"type":"keyword"},"reply_count":{"type":"integer"},"assignee":{"type":"keyword"}}}}'
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_support/_bulk?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-ndjson' --data-binary @- <<'NDJSON'
{"index":{"_id":"ticket-101"}}
{"subject":"Duplicate subscription charge","team":"billing","status":"open","channel":"email","reply_count":0}
{"index":{"_id":"ticket-102"}}
{"subject":"Invoice address correction","team":"billing","status":"open","channel":"chat","reply_count":0,"assignee":null}
{"index":{"_id":"ticket-103"}}
{"subject":"Refund progress","team":"billing","status":"open","channel":"email","reply_count":0,"assignee":"agent-7"}
{"index":{"_id":"ticket-104"}}
{"subject":"Receipt request","team":"billing","status":"open","channel":"chat","reply_count":1}
{"index":{"_id":"ticket-105"}}
{"subject":"Cannot sign in","team":"technical","status":"open","channel":"email","reply_count":0}
{"index":{"_id":"ticket-106"}}
{"subject":"Payment confirmation","team":"billing","status":"closed","channel":"email","reply_count":0}
{"index":{"_id":"ticket-107"}}
{"subject":"Missing invoice number","team":"billing","status":"open","channel":"email","reply_count":0,"assignee":""}
NDJSON
sleep 5
```

The same five-second settling pause follows writes on both endpoints; this does not establish immediate gateway refresh visibility. Find tickets needing an owner and a first reply:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_support/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":10,"query":{"bool":{"filter":[{"term":{"team":"billing"}},{"term":{"status":"open"}},{"term":{"reply_count":0}}],"must_not":[{"exists":{"field":"assignee"}}]}}}'
```

Expect exactly `ticket-101` (duplicate charge) and `ticket-102` (address correction), their complete sources, and total `2`; hit order is immaterial. Count contact channels over this same queue:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_support/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":0,"query":{"bool":{"filter":[{"term":{"team":"billing"}},{"term":{"status":"open"}},{"term":{"reply_count":0}}],"must_not":[{"exists":{"field":"assignee"}}]}},"aggs":{"channels":{"terms":{"field":"channel","size":10}}}}'
```

Expect `email: 1` and `chat: 1`, with no hits. Assign the duplicate-charge ticket:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_support/_update/ticket-101?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"doc":{"assignee":"agent-12"}}'
sleep 5
curl -fsS "$ES/field_note_support/_doc/ticket-101"
```

The update returns `updated`. The read shows `assignee: "agent-12"` while preserving the subject, team, status, channel, and zero replies. Repeat both search requests: only `ticket-102` remains, total `1`, and the sole channel bucket is `chat: 1`. Assignment alone removes a ticket from the unowned queue even before anyone replies.

The [fixture](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/fixtures/support.json) and [replay](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/support.py) check statuses, bulk results, every stored ID/source, exact search totals, channel counts, and assignment exclusion. The [recorded run](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/support-2026-10-13.json) passed 74/74 checks on Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and gateway 0.2.0 with Qdrant 1.15.5, using identical requests and default embedded-source, synchronous writes. The curl blocks were also run on both endpoints. No gateway code change or performance claim is involved.

Boundary: updates are read-merge-write, so atomic concurrent ticket claiming remains [unsupported](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/compatibility/).

Remove the example index when finished:

```sh
curl -fsS -X DELETE "$ES/field_note_support"
```

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-13-creating-an-index-is-not-a-mapping-update.md

# Creating an index is not a mapping update

Provisioning code often treats “already exists” as a narrow, recoverable race. It can do that reliably only when the server identifies the condition correctly. The gateway already rejected a second `PUT /products` before contacting Qdrant, but it grouped the request with unsupported query features and returned `qdrant_gateway_unsupported_query`. That classification could make an Elasticsearch or OpenSearch client treat a normal create race as an incompatible request.

Elasticsearch and OpenSearch implement this case independently but agree on the exception class. [Elasticsearch 9.5.5's create-index service](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/blob/v9.5.5/server/src/main/java/org/elasticsearch/cluster/metadata/MetadataCreateIndexService.java#L291-L295) throws `ResourceAlreadyExistsException` when either routing or index metadata already contains the name. [OpenSearch 3.9's corresponding service](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/blob/3.9/server/src/main/java/org/opensearch/cluster/metadata/MetadataCreateIndexService.java#L275-L279) performs the same two checks. OpenSearch also publishes the resulting REST example as HTTP 400 with `resource_already_exists_exception` in its [create/delete error-shape discussion](https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch/issues/14805).

The gateway now returns the shared client-visible shape, including a root cause, top-level exception, reason, index name, and status 400. The check runs under the existing index-administration lock and before any Qdrant request. A focused regression also proves that the original mapping remains unchanged:

```console
cargo test duplicate_index_creation_returns_native_conflict_without_qdrant_work
```

This is request-level validation with a mocked upstream request counter, not a live-engine benchmark. Cached Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 containers were available for a native probe, but the local Docker storage backend returned an input/output error before either container started. The version-specific source above is therefore the native evidence for this run. The gateway does not include a native index UUID because its metadata catalogue does not currently assign one. A different requested name that merely normalizes to an occupied Qdrant collection remains a gateway-specific `index.name` validation error rather than pretending that the Elasticsearch/OpenSearch index itself already exists.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-13-alias-add-is-not-a-retarget.md

# Alias add is not a retarget

The gateway stores one concrete index per alias. Its alias transaction used SQLite `INSERT OR REPLACE` for an `add` action, so adding an existing alias to a different index silently discarded the original target. That looked like a convenient retarget, but it changed the meaning of a standard Elasticsearch/OpenSearch request and could redirect application reads and writes without the caller expressing a swap.

A direct endpoint probe against Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 used the same five-request sequence: create `products-v1` and `products-v2`, add `current-products` to the first, add it to the second, then inspect the alias. Both native engines acknowledged both adds and returned both indices as targets. This agrees with the independent [Elasticsearch alias documentation](https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/aliases.html) and [OpenSearch manage-aliases documentation](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/api-reference/alias/aliases-api/): aliases can cover multiple indices, and a move is expressed as remove plus add in one atomic request. The sanitized [probe evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/elasticsearch-9.5.5-opensearch-3.9-alias-add-2026-10-13.json) records the versions, requests, acknowledgements, and final targets.

The gateway still deliberately supports only single-target aliases. It now evaluates the final topology of the complete action batch before opening the write transaction. An add-only request that would require two targets receives a structured HTTP 400 compatibility error, and the existing target remains unchanged. A remove+add swap remains accepted in either action order because the final topology has one target and the SQLite transaction makes the change atomically visible.

```console
cargo test alias_add_does_not_silently_retarget_a_single_index_alias
```

This is a fail-closed compatibility improvement, not multi-index alias support. The gateway does not yet merge searches across indices, select a write index, apply alias filters, or reproduce native per-action partial-failure responses. The endpoint probe measures request semantics only; it makes no latency or resource-use claim.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-12-head-must-not-hide-storage-failures.md

# HEAD must not hide storage failures

Document-existence checks have a deliberately small contract. The [Elasticsearch 8 API reference](https://www.elastic.co/docs/api/doc/elasticsearch/v8/operation/operation-exists) and the [OpenSearch Get Document API reference](https://docs.opensearch.org/latest/api-reference/document-apis/get-documents/#checking-document-existence) both describe `HEAD /<index>/_doc/<id>` as HTTP 200 when the document exists and HTTP 404 when it does not. A storage outage is neither result.

The gateway's HEAD path previously caught every Qdrant error and returned 404. A connection failure, missing collection, or Qdrant 5xx therefore looked like a trustworthy “document absent” answer. That can make health checks, conditional writes, and reconciliation jobs take destructive action on false information.

HEAD now uses the same narrow missing-point classification as GET without retrieving the document source. The known Qdrant missing-point response remains a 404, while transport failures and upstream errors return 502. All gateway HEAD routes also attach `X-Elastic-Product: Elasticsearch`, and the response body remains empty. The focused regression injects a Qdrant 503 and verifies an empty 502 response in both embedded-source and document-projection modes:

```console
cargo test head_document_does_not_hide_qdrant_failures_as_not_found
```

This validation is request-level and uses a mocked Qdrant response; it is not a live Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, or Qdrant benchmark. The native status contract comes from the public engine documentation above. Query parameters such as `routing`, `refresh`, `realtime`, and explicit version checks remain outside the gateway's current HEAD compatibility surface.


---

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-12-a-missing-point-is-not-a-failed-upstream.md

# A missing point is not a failed upstream

The Elasticsearch and OpenSearch index APIs are upserts, but their response describes which side of the operation happened. Live probes against Elasticsearch 9.5.5 and OpenSearch 3.9.0 both returned HTTP 201 with `result: "created"` for the first `PUT /<index>/_doc/<id>`, then HTTP 200 with `result: "updated"` for the replacement.

The gateway already performed a point read before this write so it could make the same distinction. Against the repository's pinned Qdrant 1.15.5, however, a missing single point returns HTTP 404 with a structured “Point with id … does not exists” error. The generic Qdrant client treated every non-success response as an upstream failure, so the very first index request returned 502 and never reached the upsert.

Single-point reads now recognize that exact missing-point response as an absent document. The shared path fixes ordinary GETs and the preflight reads used by standalone index, create, update, and delete operations. The exception is deliberately narrow: a Qdrant 404 that says the collection is missing still becomes a gateway 502, preserving a visible signal for storage/catalogue drift instead of pretending the document is absent.

The sanitized [Elasticsearch 9.5.5, OpenSearch 3.9.0, and Qdrant 1.15.5 evidence](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/elasticsearch-9.5.5-opensearch-3.9-qdrant-missing-point-2026-10-12.json) records the native contract, Qdrant response shape, and live changed-gateway results. The gateway returned 404 for a missing GET, 201/`created` for the first PUT, 200/`updated` for the second PUT, and the replacement source on the final GET. Focused regressions use the observed Qdrant error body in both source-storage modes and prove that missing collections remain upstream errors.

This is a single-document correctness check, not a concurrency or performance benchmark. The extra existence read was already part of the standalone index path, so the fix adds no request. That preflight still is not an atomic compare-and-write across gateway replicas, and the gateway's sequence-number, primary-term, and version fields remain approximate.

Source: https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/markdown/2026-10-11-travel-disruption-desk.md

# Two passengers, one cancelled departure

A travel disruption desk needs departures from York with at least two seats, either direct to London or to Peterborough for an onward connection. Six synthetic services include a one-seat departure, a different origin, an unsuitable destination, and an already cancelled train. These are illustrative inventory snapshots, not live timetables.

Use running Elasticsearch-compatible servers and a fresh `field_note_travel` index. Curl is the client: run these commands on each server, changing only `ES` to the gateway URL (for example, `http://localhost:9200`).

```sh
ES=http://localhost:19200
curl -fsS -X PUT "$ES/field_note_travel" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"mappings":{"properties":{"title":{"type":"text"},"origin":{"type":"keyword"},"destination":{"type":"keyword"},"operator":{"type":"keyword"},"seats_available":{"type":"integer"},"status":{"type":"keyword"}}}}'
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_travel/_bulk?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/x-ndjson' --data-binary @- <<'NDJSON'
{"index":{"_id":"service-101"}}
{"title":"York to London morning","origin":"York","destination":"London","operator":"North Rail","seats_available":4,"status":"scheduled"}
{"index":{"_id":"service-102"}}
{"title":"York to Peterborough connector","origin":"York","destination":"Peterborough","operator":"East Rail","seats_available":2,"status":"scheduled"}
{"index":{"_id":"service-103"}}
{"title":"York to London last seat","origin":"York","destination":"London","operator":"North Rail","seats_available":1,"status":"scheduled"}
{"index":{"_id":"service-104"}}
{"title":"Leeds to London morning","origin":"Leeds","destination":"London","operator":"East Rail","seats_available":8,"status":"scheduled"}
{"index":{"_id":"service-105"}}
{"title":"York to Edinburgh morning","origin":"York","destination":"Edinburgh","operator":"North Rail","seats_available":6,"status":"scheduled"}
{"index":{"_id":"service-106"}}
{"title":"York to London cancelled","origin":"York","destination":"London","operator":"East Rail","seats_available":9,"status":"cancelled"}
NDJSON
sleep 5
```

Both endpoints use the same five-second settling pause; this does not establish immediate gateway refresh visibility.

Find departures that can accommodate both passengers. `terms` accepts either destination; all four filters must hold:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_travel/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":10,"query":{"bool":{"filter":[{"term":{"origin":"York"}},{"terms":{"destination":["London","Peterborough"]}},{"term":{"status":"scheduled"}},{"range":{"seats_available":{"gte":2}}}]}}}'
```

Expect exactly `service-101` and `service-102`, with complete sources and total `2`; hit order is immaterial. Count operators over that same eligible set:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_travel/_search" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"size":0,"query":{"bool":{"filter":[{"term":{"origin":"York"}},{"terms":{"destination":["London","Peterborough"]}},{"term":{"status":"scheduled"}},{"range":{"seats_available":{"gte":2}}}]}},"aggs":{"operators":{"terms":{"field":"operator","size":10}}}}'
```

Expect `North Rail: 1` and `East Rail: 1`, with no hits. Now cancel the direct departure:

```sh
curl -fsS -X POST "$ES/field_note_travel/_update/service-101?refresh=wait_for" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"doc":{"status":"cancelled"}}'
sleep 5
curl -fsS "$ES/field_note_travel/_doc/service-101"
```

The update returns `updated`. The read shows `status: "cancelled"`, preserving the title, origin, destination, operator, and four available seats. Repeat both search requests: only `service-102` remains, total `1`, and the sole operator bucket is `East Rail: 1`. Cancellation must exclude the service even when its seat count still looks sufficient. The booking system must separately validate the connection and reserve seats.

The [fixture](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/fixtures/travel.json) and [replay](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/travel.py) check statuses, bulk results, every stored ID/source, search totals, operator facets, and cancellation exclusion. The [recorded run](https://github.com/dstockton/qdrant-es-gateway/blob/main/validation/evidence/travel-2026-10-11.json) passed 70/70 checks on Elasticsearch 8.15.0 and gateway 0.2.0 with Qdrant 1.15.5, using identical requests and default embedded-source, synchronous writes. The curl blocks were also executed on both endpoints. No gateway code change or performance claim is involved.

Boundary: atomic seat reservations through concurrent updates remain [unsupported](https://dstockton.github.io/qdrant-es-gateway/compatibility/).
